Absolute thrombolytics contraindications

Relative thrombolytics contraindications

Prior intracranial bleed

BP > 180/110 mm Hg

Intracranial malignancy

Ischemic stroke > 3 months or other intracranial pathology

Ischemic stroke within 3 months

Major surgery < 3 weeks or recent internal bleeding 2-4 weeks

Closed head or facial trauma within 3 months

Prolonged CPR > 10 minutes or puncture of non-compressible

Active bleeding (except menses)

vascular structure

Aortic dissection or acute pericarditis

Active peptic ulcer

Use of streptokinase or allergy to this agent (use TNK or tPA)

Pregnancy

Therapeutic anticoagulants (coumadin use)

Give 2nd antiplatelet therapy (in addition to ASA)

  • Clopidogrel if thrombolysis
  • Clopidogrel, ticagrelor, or prasugrel if primary PCI is being considered

Consider anticoagulation therapy (with thrombolysis): unfractionated heparin or LMWH (enoxaparin)

NSTEMI diagnostic pathway
Step

Considerations

Is the patient stable? Vitals?

Airway, breathing, circulation; BP, HR, RR, temperature, O2 saturation

Hx and PEx

Same as STEMI

Ix

May be completely normal; may have normal ST segments and T waves

Few develop Q waves

Early mortality is less than the STEMI population; 6-month mortality is equivalent

Patients: older, previous MI, multivessel disease, prone to re-infarction

ST depression

T wave inversion

Dx

Hx, ECG, rise and fall in troponin

Partial occlusion: thrombus (common) and/or impaired supply/demand

Management

Less urgency – do not need immediate reperfusion therapy

Control ischemia with beta-blockers and nitroglycerin

Correct any aggravating factors – hypoxia, anemia, hypotension

Pacify the plaque with anti-platelet and anticoagulant therapy to prevent thrombus propagation

  • ASA + second anti-platelet agent (clopidogrel, ticagrelor)
  • Unfractionated IV heparin, LMWH (enoxaparin), fondaparinux, or thrombin inhibitor (bivalirudin) for 48-72 hours

Control the ischemia: bed rest, oxygen, nitrates, morphine, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, ACEI

Correct any aggravating factors – hypoxia, anemia, hypotension

Risk stratification

blocks.alt: Figure from the Myocardial Infarction notes

blocks.html:
Angiography within 24-48 hours followed by revascularization as appropriate – angioplasty/stent or CABG

  • Especially those at higher risk and earlier: marked ECG change (ST deviation), elevated cardiac troponin, ongoing pain, signs of

pulmonary edema or hypotension

  • Aim of angiography is to define anatomy with a view to revascularization – PCI or CABG
Recommended medical management for secondary prevention post-MI
Therapy

Recommendations

Antiplatelet therapy

ASA

Loading dose = 162-325 mg

Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI

Maintenance dose = 81-162 mg/day and continued indefinitely

For patients also taking ticagrelor, ASA dose = 75-100 mg

Clopidogrel – use with aspirin

Loading dose = 300 mg; or 600 mg if undergoing invasive strategy in the next 24 hours

Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI

Maintenance dose = 75 mg daily for 12 months, regardless of PCI/stent procedure

Ticagrelor – use with aspirin

Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI

blocks.alt: Figure from the Myocardial Infarction notes
Figure from the Myocardial Infarction notes

blocks.html:
Beta-blockers

Initiate within 12-24 hours to all patients with MI and no contraindications

Should be continued during and after hospitalization for all patients with MI and no contraindications

↓ myocardial oxygen demand: ↓ HR, ↓ systemc BP (afterload), ↓ myocardial contractility

↑ oxygen delivery: ↓ HR, prolong diastole, more coronary perfusion time

Reduce recurrent ischemia and re-infarction – anti-ischemic, anti-arrhythmic, anti-hypertensive

Long-term mortality benefit for at least 2-3 years post-MI

ACE inhibitors

Initiate within 24 hours to all patients with MI and no contraindications, especially anterior MI, HF, and EF ≤ 40%

Initiate at a low starting dose to avoid hypotension and titrate to an evidence-based dose

An ARB should be given to patients with MI who have indications for but are intolerant of ACE inhibitors

↓ mortality following MI, slow the progression to HF, ↓ infarct expansion/LV dilatation

Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA)
Prevalence

4-5% of men between the ages of 50-79

Risk factors

Older age, male, FHx, Caucasian, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking

FHx

15-25% of patients undergoing AAA repair have a 1st degree relative with AAA

More likely in females, patients with multiple aneurysms, and younger presentations

If a patient has an aneurysm, their sibling risk is 7% for male probands and 12% for female probands

Natural

Never regress – usually either remain stable or slow growing (1-3 mm/year)

development

The larger the aneurysm, the faster it tends to grow

Saccular/pseudoaneurysms or aneurysms from a secondary cause can grow faster and rupture at smaller sizes – repair regardless of size

PEx (unreliable)

Large aneurysms are obvious, although they are often missed

Palpation can only detect 50% of aneurysms between 3.5-6 cm in size – very inaccurate for size prediction

Ix

Ultrasound: good screening test; does not give anatomic details and less accurate than CT (underestimates size by 5 mm)

CT angiogram: gold standard; fine cuts (0.625 mm); gives anatomic details and most accurate size; allows surgeon to plan therapy

Catheter-based angiography: not used; does not give a measure of true diameter (only luminal diameter); very little anatomic detail

MR-angiography: not used much; long acquisition; risk of nephrotoxicity; does not resolve calcification well; underestimates vessel size

Screening

One-time abdominal ultrasound

Men ages 65-75

Women with risk factors (FHx, smoking, atherosclerotic disease)

Men/women > 55 years with a FHx (1st degree relative)

MASS trial: 4.9% had AAA > 3 cm; 40% relative risk reduction in AAA mortality; number needed to screen to prevent 1 death = 1/276

Risk of rupture

Risk of rupture is based on the diameter (best estimate):

  • 5.5 cm = 5-10%/year
  • 6-6.5 cm = 10-15%/year
  • 6.5-6.9 cm = 15-20%/year

Prophylactic operation to prevent complications – asymptomatic (pain and embolic consequences are very rare)

Individualized decision for each patient: risk of rupture vs. life expectancy and risk of death with surgery

  • Conduit: autogenous vein (long saphenous, small saphenous, or arm veins);

synthetic (gortex)

  • Good: effective, inexpensive (unless complications arise), durable (with good
  • Good: effective (short- to mid-term), minimally invasive, outpatient

anatomy and quality vein)

  • Bad: general anesthetic, hospital stay, long recovery, wound complications
  • Bad: secondary re-interventions, increased cost
  • Ugly: graft thrombosis (thrombolysis, redo surgery), infected grafts (high rate
  • Ugly: puncture site complications (expanding hematoma, pseudoaneurysm,

Module Questions

25.What is the differential diagnosis for embolic acute limb ischemia? Cardiac (atrial fibrillation, endocarditis, myocardial infarction, prosthetic valves,

paradoxical), emboli for aneurysmal disease with chronic thrombus, peripheral vascular disease

  • 26.What is the procedure of choice if a patient develops compartment syndrome? Fasciotomyà compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency and should

be treated expeditiously with a fasciotomy to allow the muscles in the compartment to swell; if the fascia is not released, neuropathy can occur and even

muscle necrosis leading to amputation

27.What is the definition of critical limb ischemia? Rest pain and/or non-healing ulceration/gangrene

  • 28.Where is rest pain usually located in critical limb ischemia? Footà occurs in the tissue furthest from the heart, which is in the foot and toes; claudication

happens in muscle groups such as the calf

29.Which of the following (stop smoking, aspirin, exercise, blood pressure control) is the most important regarding the management of peripheral arterial

  • disease? Stop smokingà all are important for management of PAD, but smoking gives patients 3× risk of developing critical limb ischemia; the only risk

factor that is more important for PAD is diabetes, which increases the risk of CLI 4×

30.The symptom that is diagnostic of critical limb ischemia is: Rest pain

31.What is the medical management of PAD? ABCDES: antiplatelet, blood pressure management, cholesterol management, diabetes management, exercise,

smoking cessation

32.Name some options for lower extremity revascularization: Femoral-popliteal bypass, aorto-bifemoral bypass, angioplasty and stenting, axillary-femoral

bypass

Operative risk: CAD, CVD, COPD

Invasive Ix:

  • CT angiogram
  • Angiography

Medical management:

  • Risk factor modification
  • Anti-platelet therapy

Endovascular revascularization – newer approach

  • Performed in an angiography suite; local anesthetic
  • Femoral puncture, balloon angioplasty, stents, atherectomy

Meet the Patient

A 63 year old male patient presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of chest pain. He reports worsening chest pain starting 8 hours prior to

presentation to emergency department. Central chest pain currently 8/10 and radiating to his jaw. Associated symptoms include dyspnea and diaphoresis. Non-

pleuritic pain, no cough, no fevers, chills, or infectious symptoms.

History
  • PMHx: Hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, osteoarthritis
  • Family Hx: No family history of premature coronary artery disease
  • Social Hx: Truck driver, independent contractor. Ex-smoker, 20 pack-year smoking history, quit 10 years ago. No significant alcohol or drug use.
  • Current medications: HCTZ, 25mg daily; Lansoprazole, 30mg daily; and Naproxen as needed. No known medication allergies.
Physical Exam
  • Temperature = 37.6°C
  • BP = 135/90 mm Hg, no significant difference between left and right arms; HR = 64 bpm; RR = 20/min; SpO2 = 95% on room air
  • Heart sounds: normal S1/S2, no S3/S4, no murmurs
  • JVP noted at the angle of the jaw, lungs clear, trace peripheral edema is noted, normal peripheral pulses noted in upper and lower extremities
Preliminary Investigations
  • Normal CBC, electrolytes, and renal function. Cardiac biomarkers (CK, troponin) are pending.
  • Chest X-ray shows normal cardiac silhouette and mediastinum. Lung fields are clear with no evidence of consolidation or pulmonary edema.
  • A 12-lead ECG is performed which shows the following:

blocks.alt: Figure from the Case of the Week notes

blocks.html:
The baseline ECG shows which of the following (choose 3)?

  • ST elevation in the anterior leads
  • ST elevation in the lateral leads
  • ST elevation in the inferior leads – ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and AVF, consistent with inferior ST elevation
  • ST depression in the lateral leads – there is reciprocal ST depression in leads I, AVL (high lateral leads), and septal leads (particularly lead V2), which may

reflect posterior involvement

  • ST depression in the inferior leads
  • 2nd degree AV block, Mobitz I – progressive prolongation of the PR interval is noted, followed by a non-conducted P-wave, consistent with Wenckebach

pattern

  • 2nd degree AV block, Mobitz II
  • 3rd degree AV block/complete heart block

Consider this: You are working in a hospital without access to primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) on-site. Travel time to the nearest PCI capable

center is 150 minutes.

What is your next step in managing this patient?

a)

Arrange transfer to the nearest facility for primary PCI

b)

Administer fibrinolytic therapy

c)

Repeat serial ECG and wait for pending cardiac biomarkers

d)

CT head to rule out intracranial hemorrhage

e)

CT pulmonary angiogram to rule out pulmonary embolism

  • In the absence of contraindications, fibrinolytic therapy should be given to patients with STEMI and onset of ischemic symptoms within the previous 12

hours, when it is anticipated that primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Serial ECG, repeat biomarkers and further

imaging will only delay therapy in this patient in whom ST-elevation MI has already been diagnosed.

Which of the following are absolute contraindications to administration of fibrinolytic therapy (choose 3)?

a)

Intracerebral hemorrhage 5 years ago

b)

Ischemic stroke 6 months ago

c)

Lung adenocarcinoma with metastases to the brain

d)

Trauma CPR

e)

Suspected aortic dissection

f)

Dementia

g)

Pregnancy

  • Absolute contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy include: any prior intracerebral hemorrhage, known structural cerebral vascular lesion (arteriovenous

malformation), known malignant intracranial neoplasm (primary or metastatic), ischemic stroke within 3 months (EXCEPT acute ischemic stroke within 4.5

hours), suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding or bleeding diathesis (excluding menses), significant closed-head or facial trauma within 3 months,

intracranial or intraspinal surgery within 2 months, severe uncontrolled hypertension (unresponsive to emergency therapy), prior treatment for

streptokinase within the previous 6 months. The remaining are considered relative contraindications

After administration of fibrinolytic therapy, the patient is treated with aspirin, clopidogrel, low molecular weight heparin, nitrates for chest pain, and oxygen.

You arrange for transfer to a PCI-capable hospital.

Following administration of nitrates the patient becomes hypotensive en route (BP = 75/40). Emergent left heart catheterization is performed, revealing 100%

occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery with thrombus, which is successfully stented.

Left ventricular angiography shows an ejection fraction of 45% with akinesis of the inferior/inferolateral walls. JVP is noted at the angle of the jaw with positive

Kussmaul’s sign. Lungs are clear. Heart sounds are normal – normal S1/S2, no S3/S4, with no murmurs. The patient remains hypotensive with negative pulsus

paradoxus.

Which of the following is the most likely cause for the patient’s hypotension?

a)

Cardiogenic shock secondary to left ventricular systolic dysfunction

b)

Right ventricular infarct

c)

Acute ventricular septal defect

d)

Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation

e)

Cardiac tamponade secondary to left ventricular free wall rupture

  • While all of the above may be a cause of hypotension post-infarct, the combination of hypotension following administration of nitrates, distended jugular

veins with Kussmaul's sign (increased jugular vein pressure on inspiration) and clear lung sounds are indicative of right ventricular infarct. Patients with

impaired RV contractility are “pre-load” dependent and can become hypotensive in response to administration of vasodilators (particularly nitrates);

intravenous fluids are the mainstay of treatment. The absence of murmur, clear lungs fields, and absence of pulsus paradoxus make the other etiologies

less likely.

The patient is discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy (ASA, Ticagrelor) to continue for a minimum of 1 year.

Which of the following medications would provide benefit for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction in this patient (choose 2)?

a)

Bisoprolol, 2.5 mg daily

b)

Ramipril, 5 mg daily – ACE inhibitors provide benefit for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction

c)

Atorvastatin, 40 mg daily – HMG Co-A reductase inhibitors (“statins”) provide benefit for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction

d)

Amlodipine, 2.5 mg daily

e)

Ivabradine, 5 mg daily

  • Benefit of ACE inhibitors is most significant in patients who have co-existing hypertension, diabetes, left ventricular ejection fraction of < 40%, or chronic

kidney disease. However guidelines recommend ACE inhibitor therapy for secondary prevention in all patients post infarct. If ACE inhibitors are not

tolerated due to side effects (i.e. cough), an angiotensin receptor blocker is recommended.

  • Beta blockers (ex. Bisoprolol) provide benefit in patients with significant left ventricular systolic dysfunction post MI (ejection fraction < 40%) with or

without clinical signs of heart failure. Bisoprolol, calcium channel blockers and ivabradine can be effective as anti-anginal therapies, but do not provide

clear benefit in secondary prevention of myocardial infarction.

Case Follow-Up

He is referred to cardiac rehab, and asked to follow-up with his primary care provider within 1 months to review how he is tolerating his medications. Follow-up

is arranged with the cardiologist within 6 weeks’ time.

Consider this: The patient returns to your clinic for follow-up 6 weeks post discharge. He is an independent contractor and truck driver, and will be off work for at

least 3 months due to suspension of his commercial driving license following his myocardial infarction. Due to significant financial constraints, he discloses that

he has not renewed his prescriptions after discharge. He is currently taking only ASA 81 mg daily. The cost of ticagrelor is particularly prohibitive.

1.

What discussion would you have with this patient regarding his medical treatment?

2.

What changes would you consider making to the patient's treatment given his current circumstance?

3.

How do geographic and socioeconomic considerations affect the care of this patient, and patients with myocardial infarction in general?

Which of the following statements are true of the chest x-ray? Mark all that apply.

a)

  • The chest x ray provides an accurate assessment of cardiac chamber size: False à approximation only

b)

  • The chest x ray provides a good assessment of valvular function: False à no direct assessment of valve function

c)

  • The chest x ray exposes the patient to a high dose of radiation: False à minimal dose of radiation

d)

  • The chest x ray is inexpensive: Trueà widely available and relatively inexpensive

e)

  • The chest x ray can provide insights into the patients prior medical history: Trueà evidence of prior cardiac surgeries and pacemaker implants

can be seen easily on a CXR

7.

Which of the following statements are true of echocardiography? Mark all that apply.

a)

  • Echocardiography is an appropriate test for assessment of myocardial function: Trueà preferred initial imaging modality for assessment of

myocardial function

b)

  • Echocardiography provides only limited information about cardiac valvular function: False àgold standard for assessment of cardiac valve

function

c)

  • Echocardiography is the gold standard test for assessment of coronary artery disease: False à no direct information regarding coronary

patency; some indirect information may be available (e.g. abnormalities of cardiac wall motion)

d)

  • Provision of echocardiography is limited: False à widely available and relatively inexpensive compared with other tests

e)

  • Because echocardiography utilises ultrasound, body habitus has no impact on image quality: False à patient position and body habitus can

make a significant difference to image quality

8.

  • Cardiac MRI is helpful for assessing myocardial function. Trueàgold standard for assessment of ventricular function

9.

  • Cardiac CT is the test of choice for functional assessment of cardiac valvular heart disease. Falseà used to assess cardiac valve anatomy and function but

would be inferior to echocardiography and MRI for this purpose; not first choice due to radiation exposure

  • 10.Cardiac CT correlates poorly with invasive coronary angiography. Falseà good correlation between CT angiography and invasive coronary angiograms
  • 11.Stress echocardiography mostly relies upon an assessment of relative myocardial perfusion. Falseà mostly relies on a comparison of cardiac wall motion

at rest and when stress

12.Perfusion based tests may be likely to be more sensitive for the detection of coronary artery disease than tests that rely purely on the ECG or cardiac wall

  • motion assessment. Trueà based upon the ischemic cascade, perfusion abnormalities should occur prior to abnormalities in cardiac wall motion or ECG
  • 13.The absence of chest pain during a stress test means that there is no ischemia present. Falseà chest pain occurs late in the ischemic cascade after

perfusion abnormalities, cardiac wall motion abnormalities, and ECG changes

  • 14.Transesophageal echocardiography is the optimal test for assessment of coronary artery disease. Falseà this test will yield very little information about

the coronary arteries

  • 15.Transesophageal echocardiography should be performed for all patients for routine assessment of valvular pathology. Falseà invasive test; should only be

performed to answer specific questions that cannot be obtained from non-invasive studies like transthoracic echocardiography

  • 16.Transesophageal echocardiography may be helpful when transthoracic imaging quality is insufficient. Trueà patients with suboptimal transthoracic

echocardiography images, patients where very detailed assessment of the cardiac valves may be desired for specific reasons

  • 17.Cardiac catheterisation is a routine test and should be performed whenever there is any concern about chest pain. Falseà performed routinely, but only

when the attendant risks are justified and the information desired cannot be obtained non-invasively

  • 18.The risks associated with cardiac catheterisation are small. Falseà the probability of a complication is low (1/1000 of serious injury or death), but the

potential complications are very serious

  • 19.Cardiac catheterisation is only any use for assessment of coronary arteries. Falseà excellent for assessing coronary artery flow, intracardiac pressures, and

intracardiac shunts

Valvular Heart Disease
Aortic valve
  • Three cusps
  • Ventricular systole: isovolumetric contraction, followed by the opening of

the aortic valve and rapid ejection of blood into the aorta; normally opens

with a very small pressure gradient across the valve

  • Large pressure generated across valve; a lot of wear and tear over time
  • Aortic sclerosis: thickening/calcification of the valve, but without

obstruction to flow; increases with age (50% of patients over 85 years)

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Mitral valve

  • Allows the passage of blood from the LA to the LV, and prevents its return
  • Mitral annulus – fibrous ring attached to the mitral valve leaflet
  • Two leaflets – anterior leaflet, posterior leaflets
  • Chordae tendineae
  • Papillary muscles – attached to the LV

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Aortic Stenosis (most common acquired heart disease)

Aortic Regurgitation

Patho-

Obstruction to blood flow exiting the LV into the aorta

Blood flow back from the aorta into the LV due to leaking aortic valve

physiology

↑ pressure gradient from LV to aorta

Annuloaortic ectasia: dilatation of the aortic root/valve annulus

↑ afterload to LV (Law of Laplace)

  • Usually idiopathic, but may be associated with chronic hypertension

Compensatory hypertrophy:

  • ↑ risk of aortic dissection (tear/laceration)
  • Good: maintain normal afterload
  • Bad: ↓ LV compliance, ↓ coronary blood flow, ↑ oxygen demand

Chronic aortic regurgitation

  • Contractility maintained until late in course
  • Volume overload of the LV
  • LV dilatation, ↑ wall stress, compensatory hypertrophy

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
• LV systolic function well preserved initially; CHF eventually

Acute aortic regurgitation

  • Etiology: endocarditis, dissection; sudden onset
  • Dyspnea, hypotension, short murmur (may be inaudible)
  • LV normal size and compliance
  • Sudden ↑ in LV pressure; LVEDP is transmitted back into the

LA and into the pulmonary circulation – pulmonary edema

  • Emergency surgery is usually indicated
Causes

Degenerative/calcific (etiology unclear)

Leaflet

  • Pathophysiology similar to atherosclerosis; calcium deposition
  • Calcific degeneration
  • Presents later in life in 60s to 80s – wear and tear
  • Bicuspid aortic valve
  • Genetic markers for developing aortic stenosis are being identified
  • Endocarditis
  • Tx aimed at atherosclerotic regression (statins) has no benefit
  • Lupus

Congenital/bicuspid

Root enlargement (leading cause in the Western world)

  • 1% of the population, male preponderance
  • Age-related degeneration/enlargement – most common
  • Presents in 40s and 50s
  • Hypertension – can stretch the annulus
  • 1/3 AS, 1/3 AR, 1/3 clinically insignificant
  • Cystic medial necrosis – Marfan syndrome
  • Abnormal aortas, dilated, intrinsic defect in media
  • Bicuspid aortic valve aortopathy
Symptoms

ASD: angina (chest pain), syncope (fainting), dyspnea (CHF)

blocks.html:
Overall survival is 75% at 3 years; normalizes with AVR

Asymptomatic: survival similar to general population; < 1% SCD

Symptomatic: 10% SCD if angina and higher if CHF

Clinical

Systolic murmur at the base: later peak = more severe

Diastolic murmur at the border: later peak = more severe

findings

LVH with dilated LV: apex displaced down and out

S3 heart sound: CHF

S4 heart sound: stiff LV due to hypertrophy

Widened pulse pressure – narrows as CHF develops

  • Quincke’s sign: capillary pulsations

S2 heart sound: stenotic valve does not close properly, so only hear P2

  • Muller sign: systolic pulsations of the uvula

S4 heart sound: stiff LV due to hypertrophy

  • Duroziez sign: systolic murmur when femoral artery is compressed

Pulsus parvus et tardus: reduced, delayed

proximally and diastolic murmur when compressed distally

LV heave: strong apical impulse; apex may be displaced

  • Traube sign: pistol shot sounds over the femoral artery
  • Corrigan’s sign: collapsing pulse
Diagnosis

ECG: not diagnostic

ECG: not diagnostic

Echocardiogram: gold standard

CXR: can show LVH or enlarged aorta

  • Valve gradients, valve area, LV function (EF), presence of other valve

Echocardiogram: gold standard

  • Etiology, severity, LV response (EF), aortic root size, presence of

disease, LVH, aortic root size

other valve disease

Valve area (cm2)

Mean gradient (mm Hg)

Normal = 3-4

Normal < 5

Mild > 1.5

Mild < 25

Moderate = 1-1.5

Moderate = 25-40

Severe < 1

Severe > 40

  • Based on the Doppler effect

Critical < 0.6

Management

Asymptomatic: watch and wait; no clear benefit to surgery

  • More evidence of surgery indication in asymptomatic patients

Symptomatic: valve replacement surgery

  • Bioprosthetic valve: cusps constructed from porcine valve cusps or

bovine pericardium sewn onto a frame of synthetic materials;

limited lifespan (15 years), no long-term anticoagulation

  • Mechanical valve: long life expectancy; oral anticoagulation

Long asymptomatic period – good prognosis

Exertional dyspnea, fatigue – early symptoms

Symptoms of CHF come as LV systolic function starts to fail:

  • Orthopnea
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Angina can occur – low diastolic pressure, LVH

Asymptomatic: no medications have been shown to improve survival

  • Endocarditis prophylaxis historically, but no longer suggested
  • Surgery if LV is starting to fail or if LV has dilated significantly

(LVEF < 50%, LVESD > 50 mm, LVEDD > 65 mm)

Symptomatic: surgery depends on the etiology

  • Leaflets: aortic valve replacement surgery
  • Root dilation: aortic valve sparing surgery

Mitral Stenosis

Mitral Regurgitation

Patho-

Obstruction to blood flow exiting the LA into the LV

Blood flow back from the LV into the LA due to leaking mitral valve

physiology
  • Fusion of the leaflet commissures

LV systolic function well preserved initially; starts to fail over time

  • Thickening, fibrosis, and calcification of the leaflet cusps

↑ LA pressure and volume – transmitted back to pulmonary circulation

  • Thickening, fusion and shortening of the chordae tendineae
  • Rate of rise of pulmonary pressures depends on LA compliance

LV is underfilled – reduced systemic CO

  • Pulmonary hypertension will eventually develop

Pooling of blood in LA – stasis is a risk for blood clot formation/stroke

↓ LV function – reduced systemic CO

↑ LA pressure – distention and dilation of pulmonary veins

Primary: intrinsic valve pathology

RV compensatory hypertrophy – pulmonary arterial hypertension

Secondary: distortion of a normal valve by dilatation or impairment of

Distortion of RV, distortion of tricuspid valve function, RA dilatation

surrounding structures

Causes

Rheumatic fever/heart disease – most common globally (> 99%)

  • Group A streptococcal pharyngitis – autoimmune process
  • Molecular mimicry – cross-reactivity to antigens from GAS
  • Female preponderance
  • Common in developing countries – short asymptomatic period
  • Western world (uncommon) – long asymptomatic period (15 years)
  • 25% MS, 40% MS + MR, 35% multivalvular
  • Mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary
  • Diagnosis (revised Jones criteria): recent streptococcal pharyngitis

(2-4 weeks), 2 major criteria or 1 major and 2 minor criteria

Major criteria

Minor criteria

Arthritis (migratory): 60-80%

Arthralgia

Carditis/valvulitis: 50-80%

Fever

CNS involvement: 10-30%

Elevated acute phase reactants

Subcutaneous nodules: 0-10%

(ESR, CRP)

Erythema marginatum: < 6%

Prolonged PR interval on ECG

Mitral annular calcification (MAC) – aging, atherosclerosis, abnormal

calcium metabolism, chronic kidney disease

Radiation induced valve disease – late manifestation in survivors of HL

Congenital mitral stenosis

Symptoms

General: exertional dyspnea, fatigue

Symptoms of LHF: orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea

Hemoptysis: rupture of thin walled dilated bronchial veins

Symptoms of RHF: peripheral edema, ascites, congested liver

Angina: RVH, pulmonary hypertension

Hoarseness: compression of recurrent L laryngeal nerve

Symptoms may occur earlier in high output states, such as pregnancy,

anemia, hyperthyroidism, and fever due to ↑ CO and HR

Clinical

Diastolic murmur at the apex

Systolic murmur at the apex

findings

S1 heart sound: loud initially, but diminishes as the valve stiffens

Normal carotid upstroke (vs. aortic stenosis)

S2 heart sound: loud P2 due to pulmonary hypertension

S2 heart sound: loud P2 due to pulmonary hypertension

Pulse: atrial fibrillation – LA dilation

S3 heart sound: rapid filling of the LV in diastole

Malar flush: rosy cheeks due to cutaneous vasodilatation

Apical LV impulse may be enlarged, sustained, displaced – LV dilation

LHF: pulmonary congestion, poor CO

Pulse: atrial fibrillation – LA dilation

RHF: high JVP, tricuspid regurgitation, peripheral edema, ascites

Diffuse precordial lift with severe MR due to LA enlargement

Diagnosis

ECG: can show LA enlargement and atrial fibrillation

CXR: can show LA enlargement, double density/border sign,

straightening of L heart border, splaying of the carina, RV enlargement

Echocardiogram: gold standard

  • Morphology of the mitral valve
  • Ax of mitral valve function, severity, effects on other structures (LA

dilatation, pulmonary pressure, RV size/function), likely etiology

Valve area (cm2)

Mean gradient

Pulmonary artery

(mm Hg)

pressure (mm Hg)

Mild > 1.5

Mild < 5

Mild < 30

Moderate = 1-1.5

Moderate = 5-10

Moderate = 30-50

Severe < 1

Severe > 10

Severe > 50

Management

Asymptomatic: watch and wait

Normal sinus rhythm: salt restriction and diuretics if evidence of

pulmonary congestion

Atrial fibrillation: beta blockers to slow HR and ↑ diastolic filling time;

anticoagulation to reduce risk of thrombus formation/stroke

Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty: rheumatic mitral stenosis

  • Catheter through femoral artery, IVC, RA, interatrial septum, to LA
  • Balloon is blown up inside mitral valve to increase valve area
  • Only performed if less than moderate mitral valve regurgitation
  • Delays or completely avoids the need for surgery
  • Contraindications: LA thrombus, significant mitral regurgitation

Mitral valve replacement

  • Bioprosthetic valve: older, Hx of bleeding problems
  • Mechanical valve: younger, another indication for anticoagulation

Surgery to restore/maintain normal sinus rhythm – MAZE procedure

Left atrial appendectomy – reduce risk of stroke in atrial fibrillation

Acute mitral regurgitation:

  • Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture
  • Infective endocarditis with rupture of chordae tendineae
  • Acute rheumatic fever
  • Myxomatous rupture of the chordae tendineae
  • Acute dilation of the LV due to myocarditis or myocardial ischemia
  • Mechanical failure of a prosthetic mitral valve

Chronic mitral regurgitation:

  • Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous mitral valve disease)
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Rheumatic mitral valve disease
  • Cardiomyopathy
  • Ischemic heart disease

Acute mitral regurgitation:

  • Pulmonary edema – ↓ SV, ↑ LA pressure
  • Sudden onset dyspnea, hypotension, HF/cardiogenic shock

Chronic mitral regurgitation:

  • Initially asymptomatic
  • Dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, palpitations

ECG: can show LA enlargement and atrial fibrillation

CXR: can show LA enlargement, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema

Echocardiogram: gold standard

  • Etiology, severity, LV and RV size/systolic function, LA size,

pulmonary pressures

Asymptomatic: watch and wait

Blood pressure control

Diuresis for volume overload

Atrial fibrillation: rate control medication, anticoagulation

Severe MR: endocarditis prophylaxis

Surgery indications:

  • Symptomatic, severe primary MR
  • Asymptomatic, severe primary MR, mild/moderate LV dysfunction
  • Not favourable when LV dysfunction has become severe

Mitral valve repair > mitral valve replacement if anatomy is suitable

  • Obviates the need for a prosthetic valve replacement
  • No anticoagulation
  • Decreased incidence of endocarditis

Transcatheter mitral valve repair

  • MitraClip procedure
  • Expanding clinical trial evidence – Everest II trial, COAPT trial
Module Questions

20.Which of the following symptoms (angina, syncope, palpitations, dyspnea) is associated with the worst prognosis for patient with severe aortic stenosis?

Dyspnea

21.Which of the following (parvus et tardus pulse, soft S2, late peak systolic ejection murmur, loudness of systolic murmur) is not associated with severe aortic

  • stenosis on physical examination? Loudness of systolic murmurà closing of the aortic and pulmonic valves produces the S2

22.Which of the following (EF < 50%, presence of LVH, LVESD > 50 mm, LVEDD > 65 mm) is not a quantitative parameter to intervene (operate) on severe

asymptomatic AR? Presence of LVH

23.Which of the following (bicuspid aortic valve, aortic root dilatation secondary to hypertension, degenerative aortic valve, endocarditis) is a cause of acute

aortic regurgitation? Endocarditis

24.Which of the following statements are true of mitral stenosis? Mark all that apply.

a)

  • Mitral stenosis is common in Canada: False à relatively rare in Canada; most common cause globally/in developing countries is rheumatic fever

b)

  • Mitral stenosis is caused predominantly by smoking: False à conventional cardiac risk factors may contribute to mitral annular calcification, but

globally mitral stenosis related to mitral calcification is 1% of all cases

c)

  • Mitral stenosis is caused predominantly by streptococcal infections: Trueà rheumatic fever is the most common cause of mitral stenosis;

caused by an immunological reaction that occurs because of an initial infection with streptococcus

d)

  • Mitral stenosis is not related to radiation exposure: False à radiotherapy applied to the chest may cause calcification of the cardiac valves
  • 25.Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever requires the presence of 4 major criteria. Falseà revised Jones criteria requires either 2 major or 1 major and 2 minor

criteria to be present

  • 26.Skin rash is a common finding with acute rheumatic fever. Falseà erythema marginatum is one of the major criteria but is only found in < 6% of cases
  • 27.Fever is a major criteria for acute rheumatic fever. Falseà minor criteria

28.Which of the following statements is true of mitral stenosis?

a)

  • Usually presents with breathlessness: True à exertional breathlessness is the most common presenting symptom

b)

  • Is a risk for stroke: Trueà high incidence of atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis; combined with poor blood flow through the mitral valve causes

stasis of blood in the left atrial appendage, where thrombus can develop and subsequently be released to cause stroke or systemic embolism

c)

  • Causes left ventricular failure: False à can cause symptoms and signs of LHF, but the problem is in passage of blood to the LV rather than

causing an intrinsic problem with LV function

d)

  • May present earlier in the context of another illness: Trueà increased demands on the body in other illnesses cause an increase in demand

for CO; HR increases, but there is a fixed restriction at the mitral valve level, and consequently the patient presents with symptoms or signs

earlier than they might have done otherwise

29.Malar flush is due to cutaneous vasodilatation. True

  • 30.Because the mitral valve is on the left side of the heart, patients can only get symptoms and signs of left heart disease. Falseà patients with mitral

stenosis usually initially present with symptoms of LHF, but subsequently may develop symptoms and signs of RHF

  • 31.Mitral stenosis causes a systolic ejection murmur. Falseà LV fills through the mitral valve in diastole; if the mitral valve is narrowed, the abnormal sound

will be during diastole, causing a diastolic murmur

32.Which of the following statements are true when investigating someone for mitral valve disease?

a)

  • The chest x-ray is usually sufficient: False à may give clues to mitral valve disease, but does not directly assess the mitral valve

b)

  • The ECG may yield useful clues: Trueà evidence of LA dilatation and atrial fibrillation are clues to mitral valve disease, but are not diagnostic

c)

  • The echocardiogram is the gold standard: Trueà allows visualization of mitral valve morphology, an assessment of function, and clues to the

etiology of the abnormality

d)

  • Cardiac catheterisation is always required: False à routinely, valvular abnormalities are diagnosed by echocardiography or cardiac ultrasound
  • 33.Heart rate control is unimportant when treating patients with mitral stenosis. Falseà ventricular filling is essential to ultimate CO; this will be impeded

with high HR, especially in atrial fibrillation

  • 34.Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty should be tried for all patients with mitral stenosis prior to consideration of surgery. Falseà contraindicated in

calcific mitral stenosis, co-existent significant mitral valve regurgitation, and LA appendage thrombus

  • 35.Mechanical mitral valve replacement is always preferable to a bioprosthetic valve. Trueà requires uninterrupted anticoagulation, which may be

problematic in people with prior history of bleeding or the in the elderly

36.Which of the following (mitral annulus, moderator band, chordae tendinea, papillary muscles) does not affect the structure and function of the mitral

  • valve? Moderator bandà carries conduction fibres throughout the RV

37.Secondary mitral regurgitation refers to: Distortion of a normal valve due to dilatation or dysfunction of surrounding structures

38.Which of the following is false regarding the murmur of mitral regurgitation?

a)

It is characteristically a holosystolic murmur

b)

It is typically best heard at the left lower sternal border

c)

It is accentuated with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position

d)

May be soft or inaudible in acute mitral regurgitation

39.The diagnostic test of choice for mitral regurgitation is: Echocardiogram

40.Which of the following is false regarding surgical indications for mitral regurgitation?

a)

Surgery is recommended for symptomatic patients with chronic severe primary MR

b)

Surgery is recommended for asymptomatic patients with chronic severe primary MR with mild or moderate left ventricular dysfunction

c)

Surgery is generally favourable when left ventricular dysfunction has become severe

d)

Mitral valve repair is favoured over mitral valve replacement when anatomy is suitable

41.Assuming patient characteristics and anatomy are favourable, the treatment of choice for a patient with severe symptomatic mitral regurgitation with

normal left ventricular function is: Surgical mitral valve repair

Surgical Management of Valvular Disease
Surgical aortic valve replacement
  • Median sternotomy – minimally invasive approach

1.Aorta, R atrial appendage, and base of the heart are exposed

2.Cardiopulmonary bypass – placed in the distal ascending aorta or proximal arch; aorta is cross clamped

3.Aortic valve exposed

4.Cardioplegic arrest – stop the heart

5.Valve is removed, annular stitches placed through the prosthesis

6.Aorta incision is closed – sutured anastomosis

7.Finished project – pacing wires

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes
Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
• Mortality risk = 1-2%
  • Recovery: 4-5 days in hospital; 1 month recovery at home
  • Expect dramatic improvement in quality of life – complete resolution of symptoms; improved long-term survival
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
  • Femoral arterial or alternative access (subclavian, carotid, LV apex)
  • Fluoroscopic/echo guidance
  • Rapid ventricular pacing to allow accurate placing of the valve
  • Access site hemostasis

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Acute complications
  • Related directly to injury of adjacent structures: membranous septum (heart block, VSD or LV-RA fistula), anterior leaflet of the

mitral valve (mitral regurgitation)

  • Inadequate seating of prosthesis: coronary obstruction/MI, paravalvular leak
  • There is no medical therapy for severe aortic stenosis; without intervention, survival is poor
  • SAVR has excellent outcomes and is the gold standard for patients expected to survive > 5-7 years
  • TAVI is standard of care for moderate-to-high risk, elderly patients with severe AS – awaiting long-term data regarding low-risk patients
  • Treating aortic stenosis saves lives and improves quality of life

Conventional

  • Need access to the rest of the heart
  • Bypass
  • Arrhythmia procedure, ablation

Minimally-invasive

  • Provide exposure to the relevant anatomy
  • Outcomes in RCTs are equal to conventional
  • Lesser blood transfusions
  • Lower incidence of atrial fibrillation
  • Cosmetic benefits

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Myxomatous MV disease
  • Affects 2% of the general population
  • Results in leaflet prolapse

Spectrum: fibroelastic deficiency to Barlow’s

o

  • Highly amenable to valve repair
  • Can restore normal life expectancy and quality of life
Surgical candidates
  • Severe, symptomatic mitral regurgitation
  • Declining LV function
  • Dilating LV
  • New onset atrial fibrillation
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension
Quadrangular resection ± sliding plasty

A.Segment of prolapse and redundancy is completely excised

B.Sliding plasty – mobilization of the remainder of the posterior leaflet

C.Placement of an annular band to support the repair – improves durability

Other techniques
  • Triangular resection – removes less tissue
  • Neochordae reconstruction – attach reconstructed chordae to papillary muscles
  • Folding plasty
  • ‘Haircut’/resection + chordal transfer
Minimally invasive approaches
  • Avoidance of sternotomy
  • Faster recovery, shorter hospital length of stay
  • Improved cosmesis and patient satisfaction
  • Superior visualization
  • Excellent repair results
  • Can be performed with the same 3-4 cm mini-thoracotomy approach
  • Can replace tissue and mechanical valves
Videoscopic repair techniques
  • Can perform all the same repair techniques as via open sternotomy
  • Superior visualization of MV and subvalvar apparatus
  • Need to get used to different angles
  • Specialized tools – knot pusher
Emerging therapies
  • Percutaneous MitraClip

Based on edge to edge repair

o

Any prolapsing segments are attached posteriorly to the corresponding anterior segment

o

Has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with heart failure

o

Cardiovascular Outcomes Assessment of the MitraClip Percutaneous Therapy (COAPT trial)

o

showed that hospitalizations for heart failure is significantly reduced at the 2 year mark if the

patient has severe MR and they are treated with MitraClip in addition to best medical therapy

  • Transcatheter/transapical implants

Tiara (NeoVasc, Canada) – first-in-man December 2014; worldwide experience growing

o

Device sits in the mitral annulus and prevents regurgitation or opens the valve in stenotic lesions

o

At this time, there are no good transcatheter options for mitral insufficiency – many devices in development

o

  • Mitral insufficiency (myxomatous) can be repaired with excellent long-term outcomes and can restore normal life expectancy
  • Mitral valve replacement for other indications – non-repairable valves, stenotic valves, destroyed valves with endocarditis
  • Some data suggests that replacing functional mitral regurgitation is associated with better outcomes in terms of recurrent regurgitation than a repair
  • Emerging therapies will play an increasing role in management of selected patients

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes
Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Theoretical risks of prosthetic valve
  • Structural valve deterioration (SVD)
  • Non-structural dysfunction (paravalvular leak, pannus ingrowth)
  • Thrombosis, thromboembolism
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Death
  • Patient effect: survival, quality of life, inferior hemodynamics, morbidity
Mitral valve repair restores life expectancy
  • Once patients become increasingly symptomatic, the expected survival is not what they are experiencing

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Early mitral valve repair for flail saves lives
  • Flail mitral valve is associated with increased morbidity and mortality; surgery is unavoidable
  • Do not replace flail mitral valves – repair results in a longer survival (10-15 years after surgery)
  • Early surgery on a regurgitant mitral valve before the onset of NYHA III-IV symptoms is better over the long-term than medical

management – preserves survival, reduces the risk of HF

  • Mitral valve repair techniques are simple and straightforward, and are becoming routine
  • The evidence is coming that aortic valve repair will also better preserve survival

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Advantages of valve repair
  • Hemodynamics – replacement is limited by the prosthesis itself; more aortic and mitral valve area in most repairs
  • Durability
  • Lower risk of infection, thrombosis, and thromboembolism – native tissue for blood contact
  • Less bleeding complications – no need for anticoagulation
  • Insufficient valves can be commonly repaired – stenotic valves need to be replaced
  • Successful valve repair restores life expectancy and patient survival
  • Outcomes with valve repair are excellent
  • The most perfect valve is your own!
Ideal valve prosthesis
  • Long-term durability
  • Easy to implant
  • No intrinsic thrombogenicity
  • No predilection for endocarditis
  • Widely available
  • Hemodynamic characteristics similar to native valve – no increased work demand on heart, no residual gradient, near normal

flow dynamics, no hemolysis, no activation of coagulation/inflammation cascade

blocks.alt: Figure from the Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management notes

blocks.html:
Survival with tricuspid VSRR

  • 10 years: 89%
  • 15 years: 76%
  • 20 years: 70%

Survival with bicuspid VSRR

  • 5 years: 99%
  • 10 years: 91%
Valve prosthesis options

blocks.html:
Which valve for whom?
  • When valve replacement is indicated, select an appropriate prosthesis based on patient characteristics and preferences
  • 80-year-old, severe calcific aortic stenosis à TAVI
  • 55-year-old, bicuspid aortic valve à surgery, mechanical valve; Ross procedure
  • 40-year-old, dialysis dependent, rheumatic mitral stenosis à must be replaced (stenotic lesions); mechanical valve
  • 27-year-old, MV endocarditis à repair is preferable; mechanical valve (anticoagulation is contraindicated in pregnant women);

bioprosthetic mitral valves degrade faster than aortic valves, so she would only get 5 years

presyncope, and 2 years once they develop heart failure

  • 43.What are the indications for mitral valve surgery for severe mitral regurgitation? All of the aboveàdyspnea on exertion, new onset atrial fibrillation,

new dilated LV

blocks.html:
Definitions of heart failure
  • Historic physiologic definition: a condition in which the heart is incapable of maintaining a cardiac output adequate to provide

for metabolic requirements and unable to accommodate the venous return – no mention of EF (measure of heart function)

  • Clinical definition: a syndrome in which reduced heart function is associated with diminished exercise capacity, a high incidence

of ventricular arrhythmia and a shortened life expectancy

  • A better clinical definition: a clinical syndrome characterized by typical symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling, fatigue) that

may be accompanied by signs (elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, peripheral edema) caused by a structural and/or functional

cardiac abnormality, resulting in a reduced cardiac output and/or elevated intracardiac pressures at rest or during stress

  • Layman’s terms: an inability of the heart to pump sufficient blood to meet the oxygen and nutrient demands of the body
  • Compensated heart failure: asymptomatic, despite decreased pumping function of the heart – enlarged heart, ↑ HR
  • Decompensated heart failure: symptomatic; requires treatment and often hospitalization – can no longer compensate

HF is a clinical syndrome, NOT a disease – constellation of signs and symptoms + some type of structural heart disease

Clinical definition (2005) = symptoms of HF (at rest or during exercise) + objective evidence (echocardiography) of cardiac

dysfunction (systolic and/or diastolic) + (in cases where the diagnosis is in doubt) response to treatment directed towards HF

Clinical definition (2008) = symptoms of HF (breathlessness at rest or on exercise, fatigue, tiredness, ankle swelling) + signs

typical of HF (tachycardia, tachypnoea, pulmonary rales, pleural effusion, raised JVP, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly) +

objective evidence of a structural/functional abnormality of the heart at rest (cardiomegaly, third heart sound, cardiac

murmurs, abnormality on the echocardiogram, raised natriuretic peptide concentration)

Ejection fraction is NOT required to make the diagnosis of HF
Heart failure epidemiology
  • Heart failure is the fastest-growing global CVD, posing a substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic burden
  • 40 million people are affected by heart failure around the world
  • 42-50% of patients diagnosed with heart failure will die within 5 years
  • 74% of HF patients are suffering from ≥ 1 comorbidity (renal disease, diabetes, hematological)
  • 27% of HF patients are re-hospitalized within 30 days
  • HF is the #1 reason for hospitalization in patients > 65 years
  • > 600 000 people are affected by HF in Canada today… and increasing; > 50 000 Canadians are diagnosed each year with HF
  • 1 in 2 Canadians have been touched with HF
  • HF costs Canadians more than $2.8 billion/year; 10 billion spent annually on hospital costs associated with HF
  • Number one driver for unplanned hospital admission
  • HF contributes to 1.4 million hospital days/year
  • Annual deaths from HF in Canada exceed the combined total of breast + colon + prostate cancer
  • There is no cure for HF
Pathophysiology of heart failure
  • Over time, damage involving any of the major structures/systems in the heart (in isolation/conjunction with others) can result in

the development of HF – ventricles, atria, coronary arteries, valves, electrical system, pericardium, pulmonary arteries/lungs

  • Patients often develop HF after their hearts have been weakened or damaged by other cardiovascular conditions

Figure from the Heart Failure notes

blocks.html:
Stages of heart failure development
  • Stage 1: injury/induction – all at once (MI/inflammation), or slow cumulative effects (risk factors, genetics)
  • Stage 2: cellular changes – lead to anatomic changes (cardiac remodelling)
  • Stage 3: functional changes – cardiac dysfunction and physiologic responses to accommodate the damage
  • Stage 4: symptomatic HF ± acute pulmonary edema/shock – clinical signs and symptoms are always the last thing to occur

blocks.alt: Figure from the Heart Failure notes
Figure from the Heart Failure notes

blocks.html:
Renal dysfunction will also decline as HF worsens

Biventricular heart failure: both sides affected; LHF can lead to R ventricular disease

Left-Sided HF

Right-Sided HF (Cor Pulmonale)

Systolic = failure to pump
  • Reduced EF (HFrEF)
  • LV loses ability to contract normally; less ejection force; ↑ preload
Diastolic = failure to fill the ventricle
  • Preserved EF (HFpEF)
  • LV does not relax fully between beats; ↑ afterload

Most commonly the result of pulmonary hypertension arising from chronic

lung diseases

  • COPD, PE, pulmonary fibrosis, sleep apnea, myasthenia gravis, poliomyelitis
  • Causes RV dilation and RVH

Blood backs up in veins from RV in response to ↑ pressure

Swelling/congestion in legs/ankles and abdomen

AVP/ADH in heart failure
  • Circulating AVP increases in HF patients with cardiac decompensation and hyponatremia – 2× compared to healthy controls
  • Seems paradoxical: should be lower in HF due to increased atrial pressure and blood volume

Sympathetic and RAAS activation may override volume/pressure receptors and hypothalamic control of AVP release

Systolic HF (HFrEF) = volume overload

  • Eccentric remodeling caused by ↑ preload/volume

Diastolic HF (HFpEF) = pressure overload (normalizes wall stress)

  • Concentric remodeling caused by ↑ afterload/EDP

Atrial fibrillation and heart failure
  • 20% of HF patients will have atrial fibrillation, but it is unknown whether this is causal or consequential

blocks.html:
Causes of heart failure
  • Most common: MI, CAD, chronic hypertension, valve disease, arrhythmias, chronic pulmonary disease
  • Less common: idiopathic cardiomyopathy, viral/bacterial cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, pericarditis, congenital heart disease,

diabetes, thyroid disease, pregnancy, septic shock

Diseased

Ischemic heart disease

Myocardial scar, myocardial stunning/hibernation, epicardial coronary artery disease, abnormal coronary

myocardium

microcirculation, endothelial dysfunction

Toxic damage

Recreational substance use, heavy metals, medications, radiation

Related to infection – bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites

inflammatory damage

Not related to infection – autoimmune diseases, hyper-sensitivity, and eosinophilic myocarditis

Infiltration

Metastatic, non-metastatic (amyloidosis)

Metabolic derangements

Hormonal, nutritional

Genetic abnormalities

Diverse forms – hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), muscular dystrophies

Abnormal loading

Hypertension

conditions

Valve and myocardium

Acquired – mitral, aortic, tricuspid, and pulmonary valve diseases

structural defects

Congenital – atrial and ventricular septum defects

Pericardial – constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion

endomyocardial pathologies

Causes of systolic heart failure (HFrEF) – 40%
Ischemic heart

blocks.html:
disease related
(65%)

Most have a PMHx of MI or CAD – present with an infarct and heart failure

If a vessel is blocked off, areas downstream are at risk of ischemia/necrosis; cardiac remodelling results in a dilated ventricle with a thin wall

Ischemic cardiomyopathy: patients with HF and LVEF <40% who have had MI, evidence of viable hibernating myocardium, or severe CAD

  • Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of heart failure in developed countries
  • Occult disease is not an uncommon cause of cardiomyopathy – angiography in patients with unclear etiology can be helpful
  • Can result from irreversible loss of myocardium (prior MI) or reversible loss of contractility (chronically ischemic but viable myocardium)

Clinical definitions:

  • Ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy = on the basis of underlying ischemic heart disease; pathologists would refer to this as heart failure

secondary to ischemic heart disease with LV dysfunction

  • Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy = normal coronary arteries; either primary (idiopathic) or secondary (HF from Lupus)
Cardiomyopathic

Cardiomyopathy: a myocardial disorder in which the heart muscle is structurally and functionally abnormal in the absence of coronary

causes (25%)

artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease, and congenital heart disease sufficient to explain the observed myocardial abnormality

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM): ventricular chamber enlargement and systolic dysfunction with normal LV wall thickness

  • Leads to progressive HF, LV dysfunction, arrythmias, conduction system abnormalities, thromboembolism, and sudden/HF-related death
  • May manifest at a wide range of ages and usually is identified when associated with severe limiting symptoms and disability
  • Common causes: viruses (Parvo B19, HHV6, coxsackie virus, influenza, HIV), gene mutations (more common)
  • Idiopathic DCM – up to 30% may be familial/genetic
  • Inflammatory DCM – myocarditis from infectious or non-infectious agents

-Granulomatous myocarditis (sarcoidosis): an infectious agent that produces non-caseating granulomas

-Stain: inflammatory infiltrate and granuloma; striated muscle is being destroyed

  • Peripartum DCM – associated with poor nutrition and postpartum care
  • Metabolic DCM – thyroid, diabetes, hemochromatosis
  • Toxic DCM – anthracycline, EtOH, radiation, heavy metals
  • Tachycardia-induced DCM – treating tachycardia resolves the cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): walls of the ventricles thicken and become stiff; small ventricles

  • Can be inherited or a mutation

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM): walls of the ventricles become stiff, but not necessarily thickened

  • Cardiac amyloidosis: infiltrative amyloid stiffens the ventricles and affects the valves
  • Idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy: atria are massive in comparison to the ventricles
Primary valvular/

Mitral and aortic valve disease – AS, AR, MR

congenital (10%)

Chronic volume or pressure overload

Chronic MR can cause progressive cardiac enlargement and LV dysfunction:

  • Mitral valve leaks and both the EDV and ESV gradually increase
  • This will dilate the ventricle and stretch out the mitral valve annulus, worsening the cardiomyopathy

Valvular regurgitation leads to large hearts:

  • Normal heart weight = 250-300 g
  • Diseased heart weight = 500-600 g
  • Severe MR/AR heart weight = 750-1000 g (cor bovinum = “cow’s heart”)
Hypertension

Remains a major cause for HF in parts of the world; less common in the Western world with effective pharmacotherapies

Hypertension leads to two different changes on the heart:

  • Left: LVH and pressure overload à symptomatic HF with normal EF à can progress to a low EF if an MI occurs
  • Right: dilated heart with low function à symptomatic HF with low EF
Causes of diastolic heart failure (HFpEF) – 60%
  • LVEF = 45-50%
  • Wide differential
  • Constrictive pericarditis can cause structural damage to the heart à heart failure

o

  • Aortic stenosis with can have preserved EF and a hypertrophied ventricleà heart failure

o

  • Multi-vessel disease without enlargement à heart failure/ischemic heart disease

New York Heart Association classifications of heart failure
  • Functional class waxes and wanes over time as “symptom control” interferes with exercise tolerance
  • Symptoms = fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea
  • Class I (asymptomatic): cardiac disease, but no symptoms and no limitation in ordinary physical activity
  • Class II (mild): mild symptoms and slight limitation during ordinary activity
  • Class III (moderate): significant limitation in activity due to symptoms; comfortable only at rest
  • Class IV (severe): severe limitations; symptoms even while at rest
American Heart Association heart failure stages
  • Stages are progressive; once a patient advances to the next stage, they cannot go backwards
  • Stage A: at high risk for HF but without structural heart disease or symptoms of HF – patient on chemotherapy
  • Stage B: structural heart disease but without signs or symptoms of HF – LV hypertrophy, LV dysfunction
  • Stage C: structural heart disease with prior or current symptoms – clinical HF starts to occur
  • Stage D: advanced HF and death

Classification based upon heart function (EF)
  • HF recovered EF: previous HFrEF and recovered to EF > 50%

blocks.html:
Case Example

A 54-year-old male presents to the ER with severe shortness of breath at rest. Echo shows moderate RV dysfunction and severe LV dysfunction (EF ~20%). He has

a history of heart attacks in the past. He is admitted to hospital and treated with evidence based therapies. On day 7, he is discharged home feeling much better .

On follow-up with his physician 1 month later, he denies any orthopnea, PND or edema, but notices that he is still short of breath after walking 1 city block –

often having to stop and rest.

Using the various classifications, clearly and succinctly describe this patient a) when he is admitted to hospital and b) 1 month after he is discharged.

a)

Acute biventricular HF secondary to an ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF ~20%); NYHA class IV; AHA stage C

b)

Acute biventricular HF secondary to an ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF ~20%); NYHA class II; AHA stage C

Lab tests

Standard biochemical: glucose, creatinine/GFR, BUN, liver function test; serum electrolytes (Ca2+, Mg2+); fasting lipid profile

CBC, ferritin, TSH, troponin

Urinalysis (protein, infection)

Biomarkers: natriuretic peptides – elevated BNP suggests HF, low BNP rules out HF

Chest x-ray

Assess heart size and pulmonary congestion/edema

  • Cardiomegaly: a/b > 0.5

Identify an alternative pulmonary explanation for a patient’s symptoms and signs

  • Breathlessness from heart or lungs is important

Significant LV systolic dysfunction may be present without cardiomegaly

ECG
  • Normal ECG = no heart failure/HFpEF à HF unlikely (< 2% likelihood) in patients presenting acutely with a normal ECG

Abnormal ECG = HFrEF

Evidence of infarction (Q waves) that could be causing HF, LV hypertrophy

Echocardiogram

Assess LV and RV function, diastolic function, chamber enlargement, hypertrophy, pericardial disease, valvular heart disease

Common findings in HF: LA appendage thrombus in atrial fibrillation, severe RV dysfunction, severe MR

Other tests

Nuclear perfusion scan (non-invasive)

Cardiac MRI – scar burden, more precise information on ventricular function

Cardiac catheterization/coronary angiogram

Pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz) – assess hemodynamics (invasive)

Endomyocardial biopsy – send to pathology; HCM, active myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, cardiac amyloidosis, Morbus Fabry

• Goals: improve quantity and QOL; reduce symptoms and hospitalizations; coordinate patient-centered, evidence-based care
  • Seek reversible causes of HF in each patient
  • Treatment plans must account for comorbid conditions, systolic dysfunction, and presenting symptoms
  • Vaccination
  • HFrEF = evidence-based Tx
  • HFpEF = no evidence-based Tx other than diuretics à treat risk factors; control BP, HR, and diabetes
Diuretics – acute congestion
  • Essential for decongesting heart failure patients
  • Increased neurohormonal activation (RAAS pathway) to compensate for forced fluid/salt loss
  • Can lead to hyponatremia and hypokalemia
  • Use the lowest dose possible with diuretic therapy for stable symptoms and weight
  • Loop diuretics: block the Na+K+Cl– cotransporters; most potent – furosemide
  • Thiazide diuretics: block the Na+Cl– transporter – chlorthalidone
  • Combinations are used when patients do not respond to loop diuretics on their own

Module Questions

1.

What are the causes and symptoms of heart failure?

Main causes: MI, CAD, chronic hypertension, valve disease, arrythmias, chronic pulmonary diseases

General symptoms: dyspnea, fatigue and weakness, edema in feet and ascites, rapid/irregular heartbeat, decreased exercise tolerance, wheezing and

productive cough, increased urination at night, lack of appetite, nausea, difficulty concentrating/decreased alertness

2.

What is decompensated versus compensated heart failure?

Compensated heart failure: asymptomatic despite decreased heart function; compensatory measures include enlarged heart and increased HR

Decompensated heart failure: symptomatic; requires treatment and is often accompanied by increasingly frequent hospitalizations

3.

What are the NYHA classifications of heart failure?

The New York Heart Association Classifications of Heart Failure is relatively simple way to categorize the extent of heart failure. There are four

categories based on patient limitations during physical activity. The limitations are relative to normal breathing and varying degrees of shortness of

breath or angina pain. Description of the four classes range from asymptomatic patients with no limitations in ordinary physical activity (Class I) to

patients with severe limitations who have symptoms even at rest (Class IV)

4.

What are the types of heart failure? Left-sided, right-sided, biventricular

5.

How do symptoms differ in right- versus left-sided heart failure?

Left-sided: fatigue, elevated capillary wedge pressure, pulmonary congestion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, confusion, restlessness, orthopnea,

tachycardia, exertional dyspnea, cyanosis

Right-sided: fatigue, increased peripheral resistance, ascites, enlarged spleen/liver, distended jugular veins, dependent/pitting edema

6.

What are the two types of left-sided heart failure?

  • Systolic failure = ventricle pumping problem à LV loses its ability to contract; ejection fraction is reduced (HFrEF); increased preload
  • Diastolic failure = ventricular filling problem à LV does not relax fully between beats; ejection fraction preserved (HFpEF); increased afterload

7.

What are preload and afterload?

Preload: the ventricular stretch at the end of diastole; associated with venous pressure and the rate of venous return; reflects the amount of ventricular

filling and is a volume measure

Afterload: the pressure that the heart chambers must generate to pump blood during systole; affected by SVR and pulmonary vascular resistance;

depends on arterial pressure and vascular tone and is a pressure measure

What is cor pulmonale? What causes this condition?Associated with RHF and often occurs as a result of chronic lung disease or other conditions that

8.

result in pulmonary hypertension; causes increased pressure in the RA and RV which results in maladaptive remodeling of these chambers

9.

What is the difference between concentric and eccentric remodeling of the left ventricle? How does the sarcomere organization change in each case? How

do these different types of remodeling lead to systolic versus diastolic left-ventricular heart failure?

Eccentric remodeling: can occur as an adaptive response to volume overload (preload) that commonly occurs in pregnancy; physiological modeling

response can be completely reversed when blood volume returns to normal; walls of the ventricle become thinner to increase luminal area; sarcomeres

are added in series

Concentric remodeling: occurs to compensate for lack of proper filling of the ventricle (increased afterload/pressure) by increasing the thickness of the

ventricular wall which helps to normalize pressure; response to pathological stimuli; associated with HFpEF; sarcomeres are added in parallel to increase

ventricle wall thickness

Concentric remodeling can progress to maladaptive eccentric remodeling which occurs in response to increased preload (increased volume); this occurs

through cellular pathways that result in mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death; associated with HFrEF due to decreased pumping efficiency; increased

volume of the ventricle results in thinning of the left ventricular wall; sarcomeres are added in series; may be reversed to some degree with a

ventricular assist device (artificial pump)

10.How is neurohormonal regulation dysfunctional in heart failure?

The dysfunction of the neurohormonal system is a key characteristic of heart failure. The baroreceptors are dysfunctional and no longer responsive to

changes in vessel stretch. This leads to generation of afferent signals to the central nervous system (CNS) that, in turn, lead to activation of efferent

sympathetic nervous system pathways that innervate the heart, kidney, peripheral vasculature, and skeletal muscles (neural dysregulation). The

unloading of the baroreceptors also leads to afferent signals to the CNS that stimulate cardioregulatory centers in the brain. This results in stimulation

of the release of arginine vasopressin (AVP) from the posterior pituitary (hormonal dysregulation). Importantly, innervation of the sympathetic system

results in increased renin release from the kidney which in turn results in increased levels of angiotensin II. Angiotensin II causes increased sodium and

water reabsorption by the kidney as well as increased release of aldosterone (hormonal dysregulation). This is characteristic of the body’s response to

dehydration, which is not appropriate in the case of heart failure.

11.How is AVP affected in heart failure?

The sympathetic and RAAS activation may override volume and pressure receptors as well as hypothalamic control of AVP release in heart failure.

Inappropriate release of AVP from the posterior pituitary occurs due to unloading of the baroreceptors that occurs in heart failure. AVP causes

vasoconstriction and increased systemic resistance, as well as acting on the kidneys to cause increased reabsorption of fluid; this results from the effect

of AVP to increase permeability in the collecting ducts of the kidney. Together, the effect of AVP is to increase arterial resistance.

12.What are the steps for identification of heart failure etiology?

Based on clinical observations and testing, heart failure is categorized as either HF with reduced or mid-range ejection fraction, HF with preserved

ejection fraction, or HF arising from congenital heart disease. Using a decision-making flow chart, possible causes of heart failure can be considered.

Common causes of HFpEF and HFrEF/HFmEF are considered first: these include tachyarrhythmia, valve disease, known CAD or risk factors for CAD, and

LVH. In the absence of these more common etiologies, less common causes of HF are then considered. These include, for example, toxic agents,

nutritional deficiencies, genetic defects, infiltrative diseases, etc.

13.How can heart failure be treated? What are the different classes of medication?

ACEI, ARB, beta blockers: BP lowering

MRA: diuretic and BP lowering

ARNI (sacubitril/losartan)

If channel inhibitors: decreases pacemaker activity and slows HR

Vasodilators: causes SMC relaxation in vessels and decreased afterload by decreasing peripheral resistance; useful for treatment of systolic HF

Positive inotropes (digoxin): increase the force of ventricular contraction; have not been shown to affect long-term outcomes in HF patients

14.What is the connection between heart failure and arrhythmia?

Atrial fibrillation is associated with electrophysiologic abnormalities; this results in decreased cardiac output arising from increased and irregular heart

rate. This may lead to heart failure associated with decreased filling pressures which in turn can cause increased size of the right atrial chamber. This

may in turn result in atrial fibrillation. Whether the relationship between atrial fibrillation and heart failure is causal is not clear, although a significant

percentage of individuals with atrial fibrillation also have heart failure.

Module Questions
  • 15.From a pathophysiological standpoint, chronic heart failure is a manifestation of advanced heart disease: Trueà HF is a late manifestation of heart disease

of almost any cause; it is progressive and ultimately fatal over time

  • 16.A “syndrome” is a group of signs and symptoms that occur together and characterize a particular condition as a result of a specific disease process: Falseà

syndromes result in the absence of a specific disease process

  • 17.Heart failure is the most common reason for admission to hospital for patients > 65 year of age: Trueà HF has frequent hospitalization, high morbidity,

and a high mortality over time

  • 18.Symptomatic HF starts to occur in Stage B of the pathophysiological stages of HF: Falseà Stage C; more rapid progression of HF and patient prognosis
  • 19.In clinical medicine, a patient is said to have “heart failure” only when they have or have had an episode of overt heart failure: Trueà while patients may

have evidence of asymptomatic structural heart disease (e.g. LV dysfunction), prognosis is dictated by the presence of HF symptoms together with

structural heart disease

  • 20.The most common etiology for heart failure is the result of “end stage” ischemic heart disease: Trueà 65% in community
  • 21.The most common presentation of heart failure is in patients who have preserved LV function: Falseà 60%
  • 22.Some secondary causes for heart failure can cause either HFrEF or HFpEF: Trueà sarcoidosis, hypertension, hypertrophic CM (5-8%)
  • 23.“Myocarditis” is an inflammatory condition most commonly associated with an infectious process: Falseà can be infectious, toxic, or unspecified
  • 24.Heart failure as a result of ischemic heart disease is pathologically categorized as an “ischemic cardiomyopathy”: Falseà ischemic CM is a clinical category

25.Which of the following signs (PND, orthopnea, lung crackles, liver congestion/ascites) is more suggestive of right sided heart failure, as opposed to left?

Liver congestion/ascites

26.Which of the following clinical descriptions (cold/warm, wet/dry) of perfusion and congestion has the worst prognosis? Cold and wet

27.What is the approximate prevalence and incidence of heart failure in Canada? Prevalence > 600 000; incidence > 50 000/year

28.In the classic pharmacological management of heart failure, the drugs used have targeted the effects of: Angiotensin II (ACEI, ARB), sympathetic activity

(beta blockers), aldosterone (MRA)

29.Do heart failure patients with higher resting heart rates have worse outcomes than those with lower resting heart rates? Yes, lowering HR reduces

mortality

  • 30.Should all patients with heart failure be considered for an ICD/CRT or only those with a LVEF ≤ 35%? Only those with a LVEF ≤ 35%à at an increased risk

of sudden cardiac death due to ventricular arrhythmias

31.Consider how an integrated model of care could potentially improve the management of heart failure patients resulting in an associated decline in their

morbidity and mortality.

• All advanced therapies do NOT cure heart failure (even transplant)
  • At best, they trade an imminently lethal condition for a manageable one
  • It is important for patients to understand that the main goal is to try to improve symptoms that may prolong longevity
  • Patients will often die from HF itself or a complication related to HF
  • Palliative care traditionally has focused on conditions with more straightforward trajectories – cancer
  • Since HF is a more unpredictable illness, palliative care should be considered earlier, but is often considered late
  • Common to undertake a “palli-active” approach, including destination VAD, home inotropic therapies, home intravenous

diuretics, and telehomecare

Module Questions

32.Which of the following (narrow pulse pressure, worsening renal function, slow heart rate) are signs of poor perfusion due to heart failure? Narrow pulse

pressure, worsening renal failure

33.Which of the following (left ventricular assist device), implantable defibrillator, spironolactone, beta-blockers) is considered a therapy that is initiated in

end-stage heart failure? Left ventricular assist device

34.Which are criteria consistent with a patient approaching end-stage heart failure?

a)

Left ventricular ejection fraction < 20%

b)

Reduction in beta-blocker dosage

c)

Recent use of inotropic therapy

35.What are some common (> 5%) possible complications of ventricular assist device therapy? Stroke, driveline infection

36.Why is palliative care challenging in heart failure patients? The trajectory of a heart failure patient is unpredictable

  • Hypertension is the second most important risk factor for stroke, after atrial fibrillation

1) Determine that the patient with high BP has hypertension

  • Accuracy of manual BPM can be adversely affected by the device, health care provider, and patient factors

Conversation during reading, recording of only a single BP reading, no rest period before BPM, rapid deflation of the

o

cuff, rounding off readings to 0 or 5, patient anxiety in healthcare setting

  • Routine clinical BP is 9/6 mm Hg higher than the standardized BP in a research setting
  • Proper BP procedure: sit in a comfortable chair with back supported, feet flat on the floor, arm at heart level, 5 min rest period,

take first reading, take second reading, take a third reading if there is a significant difference

NEVER record a BP on an exam table or supine in a hospital bed to determine future risk of CV events

  • HBPM and ABPM predict CV risk better than OBPM – nighttime BP correlates best with future CV events

FUN FACT

One of the adaptations that humans have made to

be able to stand on two legs instead of four like

other mammals is increased afterload.

Nerves innervating the arteries in our legs cause the

vessels to constrict when we stand up so that our

blood pressure does not fall when we are standing

upright.

We can change our blood pressure beat to beat, and

our body adapts our blood pressure depending on

what we are doing.
