  • Plan for most patients to be on a 3-drug cocktail: RAAS Inhibitor (ACEI/ARB) + diuretic/dihydropyridine CCB
  • Longer-acting (thiazide-like) diuretics are preferred over shorter-acting (thiazide) diuretics
  • RAAS inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy and caution is required when prescribing to women of childbearing potential
  • As a first line choice, beta blockers are not recommended for patients aged 60 and over without another compelling indication

such as angina or CHF

  • Diuretic-induced hypokalemia should be avoided by using K+ sparring diuretics when possible (ACEI, ARB)
  • ACEI are not used as monotherapy for black patients without another compelling indication

Higher rates of low renin hypertension in black patients, so drugs that stimulate renin are preferred as first line therapy

o

Combination therapy
  • If BP does not improve on one drug, it is better to add on a second drug than double the dose of the first drug

Much more effective and fewer side effects

  • Cerebrovascular disease = diuretics, dihydropyridines, ARB
  • LV hypertrophy = anything
  • Non-diabetic chronic kidney disease = ACEI or ARB
  • Renovascular disease = do NOT use RAAS blocking agents (can cause significant hyperkalemia or further renal impairment)
  • Diabetes with neuropathy = ARB
  • Global vascular protection = statin + ASA
Effective combinations = column A + column B
  • Preferred 3 drug cocktail = diuretic + ACEI/ARB + long-acting CCB
  • Monitor for electrolyte levels when giving 2 drugs from the same column

Case Example
  • 60 year old male patient
  • Annual check-up BP = 165/95 done with AOBP and confirmed with multiple HBPM readings
  • Patient has FHx of hypertension in parents and siblings
  • No Hx of obstructive sleep apnea or other causes of secondary hypertension
  • Initial investigations all normal, S4 present

What is the best recommendation for him? (all are reasonable recommendations)

a)

Na+ to < 2000 mg

b)

Exercise at least 30 minutes, 5/7 days

c)

Lose weight

d)

Eat vegetables and high K foods

e)

Avoid eggs

Despite complying, he still has identical readings. Should we recommend medications?

  • Yesà usual office BP threshold values for initiation of pharmacological treatment for low/moderate risk is ≥ 160 mm Hg

Which of the following long-acting medications would be your preferred choice?

a)

ACEI (perindopril, trandolapril)

b)

ARB (telmisartan, candesartan, irbesartan)

c)

Diuretic (indapamide, chlorthalidone)

d)

DHP CCB (amlodipine, nifedipine)

e)

Beta blocker (bisoprolol)

What dose of the first medication would you give him?

a)

¼ dose (start low, go slow)

b)

½ dose (80% of the effect)

c)

Full dose (go big or go home)

Should you just go ahead with combination therapy now?

a)

No, it is dangerous to start two medications together

b)

Absolutely, go big or go home

c)

  • Yes, but in a low-dose, single-pill combinationà look at starting point (165/90) and target point (140/90); 25 points away = 3+ drugs
If you have to add a second drug…
  • ACEI + diuretic or ACEI + CCB
Adherence strategies
  • Provide quality information on the consequences of hypertension and the benefits of lifestyle and drug therapy
  • Ask about side effects and record any that occur
  • Tailor pill taking into a usual daily routine (same time/place/situation)
  • Simplify drug and lifestyle regime
  • Ensure regime is affordable
  • Involve family and friends in lifestyle and medication adherence
  • Maintain regular BP follow-up
  • Consider blister packing or other adherence aids
  • Consider self-measurement of BP
  • Record prescription refill dates on calendar and consider self-monitoring pill counts
Module Questions

39.When faced with a patient with high blood pressure, which of the following statements is most accurate regarding your decision to start a patient on active

treatment?

a)

If the blood pressure is above the population mean based on age, weight, and sex, treatment is beneficial

b)

The absolute blood pressure level is more important than the global CV risk of the patient

c)

Treatment should only be offered if there is experimental evidence that treatment of similar patients reduces CV risk

d)

Drugs are generally harmful, and should be avoided unless the patient asks for them

e)

Most patients can be managed with healthy behaviours and one medication

40.Which of the following are preferred combinations of medications for the average patient with hypertension?

a)

Diuretic with calcium channel blocker

b)

ACE inhibitor with betablocker

c)

Angiotensin blocker with spironolactone

d)

ACE inhibitor with diuretic

e)

Betablocker with any inhibitor of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

41.In low CV risk patients, the current guidelines recommend that treatment not be initiated until systolic BP is over 160mmHg, whereas in high risk patients

the treatment threshold can be as low as 130mmHg. Do you believe that the wide variation in threshold blood pressures is warranted? Why or why not?

Recommendations are based on hypertension treatment trials that last at most 7 or 8 years. In low risk patients it is impossible to get enough outcome

events to show the benefit of treatment until the blood pressures are quite high.

BP Drug Treatment for the Average Patient (Dr. George Dresser, YouTube)
Step 1: RAAS inhibitor – ACEI vs. ARB
  • What are the odds that the patient will end up complaining of a cough while they are on treatment?
Step 2: Synergy and side-effects – diuretic vs. CCB
  • Look at serum K+ concentration and volume status (pedal edema)

blocks.alt: Figure from the Treatment of Hypertension notes

blocks.html:
Step 3: More synergy and side-effects – diuretic or CCB
  • Add on the drug that was not added on in step 2

Step 4: Spironolactone (MRA) vs. doxazosin (alpha 1 receptor antagonist) vs. beta blockers

  • Look at serum K+ concentration and heart rate
Step 5: Monitor
  • This 4 drug cocktail is 95% effective at controlling blood pressures in the average patient
  • If your patient is not achieving average, they are either a very exceptional patient or they are simply not taking their medication
  • Direct observe therapy: bring the patient into the clinic, hook up an ABP monitor, directly observe them taking the 4 agents and monitor their BP carefully

for 4-6 hours to verify that if in fact they are taking their medications and they are not getting an adequate BP response

Step 6: Beta blocker vs. doxazosin
  • Based on serum K+ and kidney function
  • Poor kidney function à shift into an algorithm that is more appropriate for patients with renal impairment
  • K+ > 3.7 mmol/L à give more thiazide-like diuretic
  • K+ < 3.7 mmol/L à increase the spironolactone dosing
Monitor patients for symptoms

25.Common causes of atrial fibrillation include: Hypertension, congestive heart failure due to prior MI, mitral regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse,

  • pericarditis, agingà almost any cardiac condition and some non-cardiac conditions can contribute to atrial fibrillation

26.The CHADS2 score is an acronym for calculating a patient’s stroke risk due to atrial fibrillation. What is the CHADS2 score of the following patient; a 72 year-

old man with atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, but no history of myocardial infarction or other heart disease. Does he need anticoagulation?

  • CHADS2 score of 2, he needs anticoagulationà hypertension, diabetes; any patient with a CHADS2 score > 1 should be given anticoagulation unless there

is a strong contraindication

27.The same man as in the question above comes in the Emergency Department in atrial fibrillation at 125-135bpm. He is anxious and uncomfortable with

palpitations and mild dizziness. His BP is 100/65. When asked, he really does not know when the atrial fibrillation started or how long it has been

continuing. He is on no medication. Each of the following would be reasonable treatment except:

a)

IV metoprolol

b)

IV diltiazem

c)

Oral metoprolol

d)

  • Cardioversionà patients can develop thrombus in the left atrium, especially in the left atrial appendage, as early as 48 hours after the start of

atrial fibrillation; unless the history has a clear and believable onset of symptoms less than 48 hours prior, or if the patient is already on

therapeutic anticoagulation, cardioversion raises the risk of thrombus dislodgement and stroke; if the patient is already on therapeutic

anticoagulation, then the risk of thrombus is low and cardioversion would be reasonable

• Antiplatelet agent and emergent PCI might be the most reasonable next step; if PCI not available thrombolysis is reasonable

You are asked to see a patient in the morning waiting for liver transplant assessment. They underwent a transvenous liver biopsy yesterday; now vitals have

suddenly changed:

  • HR = 178 bpm, BP = 86/56, breathing comfortably on nasal prongs with good oxygen saturation, temperature = normal
  • Blood glucose = normal
Is this patient…
  • Stable? à drugs
  • Unstable? à electricity (cardioversion/defibrillation)
  • Dead? à CPR + electricity + drugs
• Adenosine to help diagnose and convert to a sinus rhythm

Case Example 3

You are on the Internal Medicine service – there is a call for a patient with a rapid heart rate. You ask for an ECG and hurry up to the floor. The patient is a 76

year old man with a heart rate of 146, irregularly irregular. BP = 148/72. The patient has just undergone an open reduction internal fixation (ORFI) of a hip

fracture under general anesthetic.

  • PMHx: chronic atrial fibrillation (5+ years), prior NSTEMI and hypertension; no Hx of heart failure
  • Medications: metoprolol, ASA, ACEI, statin, DOAC – may have missed some medications over the last day
  • Vital signs: HR= 145 bpm, BP = 140/78, breathing comfortably on nasal prongs at 2 L/min (this is not much oxygen), afebrile
  • Tells you he has no chest pain or shortness of breath, and wonders what the ‘fuss is about’
Is this patient…
  • Stable? à drugs
  • Unstable? à electricity (cardioversion/defibrillation)
  • Dead? à CPR + electricity + drugs

This patient has chronic atrial fibrillation. This is a fairly fast rate – so we should consider slowing it down. Options:

a)

  • Adenosine à slow down pre-existing AF, then would wear off

b)

  • Verapamil à slow rate down

c)

  • Diltiazem à slow rate down

d)

  • Digoxin à slow rate down, but need to give a loading dose; not the best choice

e)

  • Metoprolol à already takes chronically and tolerates

f)

  • Amiodarone à slow rate down
Case Example 4

You are called as part of the Code Blue (Cardiac Arrest) team. A patient has collapsed. What is the most immediate therapy?

Is this patient…
  • Stable? à drugs
  • Unstable? à electricity (cardioversion/defibrillation)
  • Dead? à CPR + electricity + drugs

What is the rhythm on the monitor? Wide complex polymorphic tachycardia – Torsades de Pointes

The patient is back to sinus rhythm. On review of the chart:

  • Potassium = 3.2 meq/L (normal is 3.5-5.5)
  • Medications: methadone (chronic opioid use), haloperidol (antipsychotic started 2 days prior for delirium), levofloxacin (antibiotic started yesterday)

Precipitated an arrhythmia with electrolyte abnormalities and medications that can contribute to long QT, resulting in Torsades de Pointes

• Check the baseline ECG following return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and identify QT
  • Consider Mg2+
  • Correct K+ (slowly!)
  • Stop medications that may be contributing to prolonged QT – exception is methadone (withdrawal symptoms)
  • Increase the patient’s baseline HR – as HR increases, QT decreases

  • 28.Which of the following medications (lidocaine, verapamil, digoxin, metoprolol) would NOT slow ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation? Lidocaineà only acts

on ventricular myocytes and is not effective for supraventricular arrhythmias

You are called to see a patient following an overdose of Amitriptyline. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant medication (TCA) (Elavil®). Amitriptyline has a

very large volume of distribution (Vd), so drug levels don’t reflect toxicity, and that also means it cannot be dialyzed out as a method to treat overdose. Tricyclic

antidepressants (TCAs) such as amitriptyline have the following effects with toxicity due to overdose:

  • Na+ channel blockade
  • Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) effects
  • Alpha adrenergic receptor blockade
  • Antagonism of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors in the brain which causes seizures

29.What effect will Na+ channel blockade with TCA poisoning have on the ECG? Increased QRS

30.What will be the effect of muscarinic receptor blockade? Dilated pupils (mydriasis)

  • 31.What will be the effect of adrenergic alpha receptor blockade? Hypotension (low blood pressure) à alpha receptors cause vasoconstriction; blockade

leads to vasodilation

It is actively bleeding. Vitals are: HR = 148 bpm, BP = 78/56, RR = 28. The patient is cold and clammy with decreased capillary refill. A rhythm strip is below.

Congenital heart disease: any alteration in the structural development of the heart

  • Most common congenital defect affecting 1% of all births, not including bicuspid aortic valve and smaller muscular VSDs

  • Day 14: primary heart field is arranged in a crescent shape on the cranial side of the embryo

Fetal circulation
  • Goals: get oxygenated blood from the placenta to the coronary arteries and brain; avoid damage to non-aerated lungs
  • Shunts bypass the lungs (in parallel) and direct oxygenated blood to the head/heart and deoxygenated back to the placenta
  • 100% of the blood goes to the body, but only 10% goes to the lungs
  • Ductus venosus – oxygenated blood from the placenta bypasses hepatic circulation
  • Foramen ovale – oxygenated blood from the placenta bypasses the right heart
  • Ductus arteriosus – deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the descending aorta
What can go wrong?
  • Looping stage: different connections between atria, ventricles, and great arteries; different orientations of the heart
  • Septal stage: septal defects “holes in the heart” (ASD, VSD)
  • Later stages: valve stenosis/regurgitation, abnormal venous connections, abnormalities of the distal aorta and pulmonary artery
  • Persistent fetal circulation: patent shunts

Cardiac hemodynamics
  • Hemodynamic impact of shunt lesions depends on pressure gradient (location), resistance of

capillary beds (PVR/SVR), and resistance of hole/tube (radius, length)

Approach to congenital heart disease
1) Pink (acyanotic) or blue (cyanotic)
  • Deoxygenated Hb has a blue tone; oxygenated Hb has a red tone
  • Patients will appear cyanotic if deoxygenated Hb > 5 g/dL in the systemic circulation
  • Must have deoxygenated blood in systemic circulation to be blue
  • Requires desaturation, but will be less prominent in patients with anemia
2) Degree of pulmonary blood flow (PBF)
  • Increased PBF = lighter lungs (fluid); vascular markings extend to the lung’s edges; proximal

branch pulmonary arteries are more prominent

  • Decreased PBF = darker lungs; proximal branch pulmonary arteries look smaller (less blood)

Single ventricle lesions are not curative, but palliative surgery is offered to get them to adulthood

o

  • Medication: prostaglandin

Keeps PDA open, which ↑ PBF

o

Helpful if cause of cyanosis is ↓ PBF – tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot

o

Case Example

Ali is a 1 month male is sent to the emergency department by his GP for a heart murmur and cyanosis. No other information was provided.

History

You ask about potential symptoms of congestion – the patient has been feeding and growing normally and there is no increased work of breathing. The patient

was incidentally noted to have a murmur and some ‘duskiness’ at their 1 month check. There is no significant medical history. His development is normal. There

were no concerns with the pregnancy. There is a family history of congenital heart disease including Tetralogy of Fallot in a maternal uncle and a VSD in the

sister.

Physical Exam

What are the two most important next steps in completing your assessment?

  • General inspection of the child – assess the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation)
  • Obtain a set of vital signs – BP, HR, RR, oxygen saturation

The patient appears well and in no respiratory distress. The vital signs are within normal except for the oxygen saturation (86% on room air). Cardiac exam

reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla and back. The rest of the cardiac exam is unremarkable. The

respiratory exam is normal.

You do not have access to an echocardiogram. What investigation would you order next? Why?

  • Chest x-rayà will help determine if the patient has decreased or more normal pulmonary blood flow, and if there is more subtle lung pathology

contributing to presentation

What is the most likely diagnosis?

a)

Isolated ventricular septal defect

b)

Obstructed TAPVR

c)

Transposition of the great arteries

d)

  • Tetralogy of Fallotà murmur of pulmonary stenosis, decreased pulmonary blood flow, most common cyanotic CHD; heart looks like a “boot”

e)

Bicuspid aortic valve

Tetralogy of Fallot: decreased PBF, pulmonary outflow tract obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, eventual RVH

What would you do now?
  • Refer to pediatric cardiology for complete assessment and echocardiogram
  • Patient will need surgery around 4-6 months of life
  • They will need to be followed for progressive desaturation and tet spells

42.A 3-month-old patient presents with a pansystolic murmur. Their parents are worried about poor weight gain. They have moderate increased work of

breathing and tachypnea. In addition to their murmur, on exam the precordium is hyperdynamic and the liver is enlarged. What is the most likely

diagnosis?

a)

  • Atrial septal defect à no pansystolic murmur or congestion

b)

  • Small muscular VSD à no congestion

c)

Moderate perimembranous VSD

d)

  • Bicuspid aortic valve à no pansystolic murmur or congestion

e)

  • Patent ductus arteriosus à continuous murmur ± congestion

43.You are on call in the NICU. You are consulted for a 12-hour-old baby that appears ‘dusky.’ The neonate is in minimal distress, but their oxygen saturation is

65%. The rest of the exam is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

a)

  • Transposition of the great arteriesà most common congenital heart disease that presents in newborns; no significant murmur, severe cyanosis

b)

  • Total anomalous pulmonary venous return à presents later with less significant cyanosis

c)

  • Sepsis à cyanosis, but increased work of breathing

d)

  • Pneumonia à cyanosis, but increased work of breathing

e)

  • Hypoplastic left heart syndrome à single ventricle lesion that presents with decreased cardiac output
Pediatric Heart Murmurs
Scope of the problem
  • Heart murmurs are extremely common in children
  • Up to 80% of children have murmurs at some point in childhood; 98-99% of murmurs are not associated with CHD
  • These INNOCENT murmurs are benign/normal sounds usually caused by blood being ejected out of a NORMAL heart
  • Murmurs cause significant parental and clinician anxiety
  • GPs need the tools to distinguish an innocent murmur from a pathologic murmur and counsel families appropriately
  • Referral for murmurs is common; most referred murmurs are innocent
  • Many normal murmurs can be diagnosed after careful history and physical exam
  • Many studies show that pediatricians and neonatologists can diagnose murmurs with reasonable accuracy
Step

Considerations

Hx

Infant and toddler:

  • Increased work of breathing (especially with feeds), frequent/severe respiratory infections
  • Feeding and growth difficulties (excessive diaphoresis, lethargy/tiring with feeds), failure to thrive (low weight for height)
  • Cyanosis, activity level, loss of consciousness

Older child and adolescent:

  • Chest pain, palpitations
  • Dyspnea, cyanosis
  • Syncope, presyncope
  • Malaise/lethargy, exercise intolerance

Pregnancy exposures, FHx for pediatric and congenital heart disease, PMHx, dietary Hx

PEx

Full cardiac exam

  • Inspection of the child and precordium (distress, perfusion, dysmorphisms)
  • Palpation of the precordium (PMI, heaves, thrills) and pulses (ALWAYS check femoral pulses for aortic coarctation)
  • Auscultation – normal heart sounds, extra heart sounds, systolic murmurs, diastolic murmurs

Step-by-step auscultation

  • S1 à S2 ± splitting
  • Systole (murmurs and extra sounds) à diastole (murmurs and sounds)
  • All of these should actively be addressed in your mind prior to removing your stethoscope
  • Listen for: timing and type, location and radiation, quantity and quality, changes with different positions (maneuvers),

associated abnormalities (extra heart sounds, abnormal palpation)

Hints for auscultating children

  • Know what you are listening for
  • Be patient: leave your stethoscope on the chest and wait for crying to stop or breathing to be ‘filtered out’
  • Be opportunistic: listen first (as long as you do not forget the rest)
  • Be deliberate and active: listen specifically for all heart sounds and murmurs while stethoscope on the chest
  • Practice

Respiratory exam, hepatomegaly

Pediatric Cardiology Case 1

A 3-year-old male is referred for a heart murmur.

History
  • Patient recently seen by a new doctor
  • No parental concerns; no obvious symptoms; no relevant history
  • Murmur incidentally auscultated; rest of physical exam normal
  • Murmur described as: systolic ejection murmur; vibratory, low pitched quality, 2/6 intensity; left lower sternal border with minimal radiation; murmur

becomes louder with supine position

What is the most likely cause of this murmur?

a)

  • Pulmonary stenosis à harsh with click

b)

  • Innocent murmurà Still’s murmur

c)

  • Ventricular septal defect à pansystolic

d)

  • Aortic regurgitation à diastolic

e)

  • Patent ductus arteriosus à continuous
Pediatric Chest Pain

blocks.alt: Figure from the Congenital Heart Disease notes

blocks.html:
• Normal children do not have heart attacks – some populations may be at higher risk depending on other medical problems
  • Growing pains are common; muscle and bones often hurt
  • Rib cage is more cartilaginous in children with ossification occurring in adolescence
  • Most parents worry that chest pain = heart attack!
Step

Considerations

Hx

Aggravating and alleviating features – exercise vs. rest/other, movements, breathing

Quality (often difficult for pediatric patients to describe), quantity, location (discrete vs. vague), associated symptoms

FHx, PMHx

PEx

Reproducible pain

Cardiac abnormalities – extra heart sounds, murmurs

Non-cardiac abnormalities – signs of respiratory conditions (wheeze)

Pediatric Cardiology Case 2

A 10-year-old female is referred for chest pain.

What would suggest a cardiac cause for pediatric chest pain?

a)

  • The pain only occurs with activity (and never occurs at rest)àconsistent pain is a hallmark of cardiac chest pain

b)

  • The pain is sharp and left sided à MSK pain

c)

  • The pain is easily reproduced with palpation à MSK pain

d)

  • The pain wakes the patient from sleep à non-specific

e)

  • The patient also has a systolic murmur à common in innocent murmurs

• Acute, self-limited febrile illness
  • Unknown cause – query abnormal immune reaction to infectious trigger
  • 21/100 000 children – most common acquired pediatric heart disease in the developed world
  • At risk: children < 5 years; males > female (1.5:1); Asian (especially Japanese) = highest risk, Caucasian = lowest risk
Diagnostic criteria – clinical diagnosis
  • At least 4-5 days of fever and 4/5 clinical features

Bilateral, non-purulent conjunctivitis

o

Mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips)

o

Rash

o

Indurated, red hands and feet

o

Unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm

o

Phases of Kawasaki disease
Acute Phase

0-9 days

Microvascular angiitis, acute endarteritis

Classic symptoms

Laboratory abnormalities: thrombocytopenia, aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria, CRP elevation

Rarely: heart failure, dysrhythmia

Subacute phase

2nd– 4th week

Panvasculitis of coronaries with aneurysms and thrombus formation

Symptoms: desquamation of hands/feet; fever resolves

Laboratory: thrombocytosis

Convalescent phase

1 month-4 years

Scarring, stenosis, calcification, recanalization of coronaries

and chronic phase

Fibrosis of myocardium

CRP normalizes

Risk of coronary artery aneurysms
  • Prior to treatment of Kawasaki Disease, 25% risk of aneurysms
  • With appropriate treatment (within 10 days of fever onset), 4% risk of aneurysms
  • Asian (Japanese) > Hispanic > Caucasian > African
Treatment to prevent coronary complications
  • IVIG – reduces risk of aneurysm formation
  • ASA – benefit of preventing clots
Treatment if coronary complications
  • Ongoing antiplatelet agents; anticoagulation
  • Exercise restrictions and life-long follow-up
  • Potential need for coronary stenting/CABG
Pediatric Cardiology Case 4

A 5-year-old female presents with a persistent fever.

History
  • Fever started 6 days ago and has been persistent (with response to acetaminophen)
  • Parents are ‘at their wits end’ due to how fussy she is
Physical Exam
  • Child appears miserable and fussy but not in extremis
  • You palpate a single large (2 cm) lymph node in the left cervical chain (mobile, mild discomfort)

In addition you notice the following:

  • Red sclera (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis)
  • Lips and tongue are cracked/dry (look like the surface of a strawberry)
  • Diffuse, non-specific erythematous rash

Diagnosis
  • Kawasaki disease

Case Example

Budi is a 6 year old male who was referred for a murmur. No other information was provided.

History
  • You ask about the history of the murmur

It was incidentally detected on a routine health check

o

There are no other concerns

o

  • You still ask about the most important pediatric cardiac symptoms

There is no: chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, cyanosis, syncope, presyncope

o

His baseline energy level is normal

o

His exercise/activity level is normal

o

  • There is no significant medical history. His development is normal. There were no concerns with the pregnancy. He has a normal diet.
  • There is no family history for congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, heart failure, early coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac/unexplained deaths
Physical Exam

You move on to a full cardiac exam, including general inspection of the patient and precordium, vital signs, palpation of the chest and pulses, and of course

auscultation. You plug your stethoscope in and hear some things…

What descriptive words can you use to describe the heart murmur?
  • Timing – systolic, diastolic, continuous
  • Type – systolic (ejection/crescendo-decrescendo, pan-systolic); diastolic (early, mid, late)
  • Intensity/quantity – 1-6
  • Quality – harsh, blowing, musical
  • Location, radiation, changes with maneuvers

The murmur is a 2/6 continuous murmur heard just superior to the right clavicle. The murmur disappears when the stethoscope is pressed firmly against the

neck and when the patient lies down. What is the cause of the murmur?

a)

Peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis

b)

Stills murmur

c)

Venous hum

d)

Aortic stenosis

e)

Patent ductus arteriosus

You diagnose OM with a venous hum. What are your next steps?

a)

Reassure the child and parents that no further intervention is required

b)

Refer to cardiology

c)

Obtain an ECG

d)

Restrict from all physical activity

e)

Send to the emergency department to start initiation of beta blocker treatment

Meet the Patient

A 45 year old male presents to the ER complaining of dyspnea. He is short of breath at rest and has noticed worsening dyspnea on exertion the last 3 weeks. He

also complains of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), orthopnea, and ankle edema. No chest pain, cough, or sputum production. His past medical history is

unremarkable other than his ongoing smoking.

Physical Exam
  • BP = 90/70 mm Hg; HR = 100 bpm; O2 saturation = 90% on room air
  • CVS: normal S1 and S2 heart sounds, S3 present; grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at apex; JVP = 7 cm ASA
  • Chest: crackles at bases
  • Abdomen: soft, nontender, no organomegaly, normal bowel sounds
  • 2+ bilateral peripheral edema with cool extremities

Select the most appropriate next investigations for this patient (choose ALL that apply)

a)

CBC, electrolytes, Bun/Cr

b)

ECG

c)

Chest x-ray

d)

BNP

e)

Spirometry

f)

CT chest

g)

Echocardiogram

Investigations

blocks.alt: Figure from the Kawasaki Disease notes
Figure from the Kawasaki Disease notes

blocks.html: • The ECG demonstrates septal Q waves in V1-V3, suggestive of an old anterior myocardial infarction

blocks.alt: Figure from the Kawasaki Disease notes

blocks.html:
• The chest x-ray demonstrates vascular redistribution along with fluid in the fissure, most likely in keeping with congestive heart failure
What should be the initial therapy for this patient?

a)

  • Supplemental oxygen and IV diureticsà the patient is clinically in heart failure and requires relief of congestion with an IV diuretic like furosemide; he is

hypoxic and needs supplemental oxygen

b)

  • Beta blocker à contraindicated in Class IV heart failure, as they can lead to hemodynamic compromise

c)

  • Anticoagulation with heparin à at present the ECG suggests an old MI and the troponin is negative; the patient does not complain of chest pain and there

is no need for anticoagulation

d)

  • Spironolactone à would typically not be used in the acute setting and one would wait to demonstrate a reduced EF < 40%

The clinical description of this patient that also portends the worse prognosis would be:

a)

Warm and dry

b)

Warm and wet

c)

Cold and dry

d)

Cold and wet

  • This patient is “cold and wet” suggestive of cardiogenic shock. The “cold” refers to the cold extremities that are suggestive of a high systemic vascular

resistance (SVR) or low cardiac index (CI) that are in keeping with poor tissue perfusion. The “wet” refers to the fact the patient is volume overloaded and

congested as evidenced by an elevated JVP, lung crackles, third heart sound (S3), the BNP, and CXR findings. The combination of “cold and wet” is clinically

associated with a poor prognosis.

blocks.alt: Figure from the Kawasaki Disease notes

blocks.html:
Echocardiogram results
  • Severely dilated left ventricle with reduced systolic function; EF 25% with akinetic septum and apex; no evidence of thrombus
  • Normal right ventricular size and function
  • Mild mitral regurgitation

Which of the following would be options if the patient does not respond to initial therapy?

a)

Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP)

b)

Inotropes

c)

Left ventricular assist device (LVAD)

d)

Transplantation

  • All of the mentioned strategies are possibilities. One would start with inotropes (such as milrinone or dobutamine) to improve cardiac output and

perfusion. If such fails, then the next step would be mechanical circulatory support (MCS) with an IABP – most helpful if the patient is having ischemia. If

the patient continues to deteriorate, emergency consideration can be given to an LVAD or listing the patient for transplantation.

The patient responds well to IV diuretics and is hospitalized for a week, losing 15 lbs of weight, and feeling much better. Initially he requires milrinone, but this is

discontinued.

Given that he has HFrEF < 40%, which medications are associated with an improved mortality? (check all that apply)

a)

ACE inhibiters

b)

ARNI (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors) – sacubitril/valsartan

c)

Beta blockers

d)

Spironolactone

e)

  • Digoxin à reduces hospitalization in patients with HFrEF however does not have a mortality benefit; all other agents mentioned have a proven mortality

benefit and are part of standard guideline suggested medical therapy for patients with HFrEF

f)

Ivabradine

Follow-Up

The patient is started on guideline-directed medical therapy and discharged from hospital with a flexible diuretic regimen. He is referred to the outpatient Heart

Failure Clinic for close follow-up. Follow-up is arranged with his primary care provider in 1 week, with a requisition for bloodwork given to re-assess his

electrolytes and renal function on his current medications.

Step

Considerations

Hx

Key features of palpitations – what do they feel like (fast? Irregular?), onset and offset, triggers, actual heart rate if measured

PEx

Not particularly helpful – usually not having palpitations while in clinic

Ix

Try to capture rhythm while symptomatic

Resting ECG may be normal but may show certain patterns predisposing to arrhythmia

ECG during palpitations would be diagnostic

Longer-term rhythm monitoring

  • Holter monitor: 2 lead continuous ECG for 24-48 hours (rarely 1-2 weeks)
  • Longer-term continuous or intermittent monitors that can last for 3-8 weeks
DDx

Sinus tachycardia – exercise, anxiety, presyncope (dehydration, position changes, prolonged standing), organic (hyperthyroid, hypertension)

Sinus rhythm – increased awareness of normal heart rate

Supraventricular tachycardia

Ventricular tachycardia is more likely to present with syncope rather than palpitations

• Low perfusion at rest (COLD)
  • Cold + wet = cardiogenic shock

blocks.html:
• If someone is approaching end stage HF, they will tell you – I NEED HELP

I

Inotropes

Previous or ongoing use of dobutamine, milrinone, or dopamine

N

NYHA class/natriuretic peptide

Persistent NYHA III/IV symptoms or persistently high BNP

E

End-organ dysfunction

Worsening liver or renal function

E

Ejection fraction

Very low EF (< 20%)

D

Defibrillator shock

Recurrent shocks/ATP for VT/VF

H

Hospitalizations

≥ 2 heart failure hospitalizations in 12 months

E

Edema/escalating diuretics

Persistent edema or frequent adjustments in diuretic dosing

L

Low blood pressure

Consistently low systolic BP (< 90 mm Hg)

P

Prognostic medications

Need to reduce/inability to uptitrate goal-directed therapies

  • Once the patient has been identified as having advanced HF, a referral can be made to a center providing advanced care
  • This care can include mechanical devices (ventricular assist devices) or transplant
  • Being referred or seen at a transplant centre does NOT mean the patient is “listed” – one of the options will be considered
  • Very few patients with advanced HF will meet criteria for transplantation – only 50 people on the waitlist in Ontario

Patients approaching Stage D

  • Recognize your limits as a physician in treating a

complex condition

  • Allow your patient to be considered for specialized

therapies that are usually concentrated in a few

centres

  • Inform your patient about the seriousness of their

condition and provide information about prognosis

and outcomes

Inotropic therapy
  • Although most therapies in HF are used to slow or even reverse progression of disease, there is a point beyond which these

therapies may be of no benefit – cold patients

  • Beta-blockers may not be of benefit at this stage due to their inherent negative inotropic nature, which tries to preserve

ventricular function

  • Consider reducing these medications with the realization that this represents an advancing disease state
  • Inotropic therapy improves overall symptoms, but does NOT prolong life and may precipitate arrhythmogenic events
  • Inotropy is considered as a bridge to a more durable therapy (transplantation/LVAD) or as palliation

• Orthotopic transplantation: the recipient’s heart is explanted with a new donor heart being implanted in its place
  • Heterotopic transplant: the recipient’s heart is left in situ and a donor heart is placed in series

blocks.html:
Components of transplant assessment

1.Does the patient want transplant/advanced options?

2.Is the patient’s condition advanced enough to warrant transplant?

Severe symptoms supplemented by cardiopulmonary exercise testing and invasive hemodynamics

o

3.Any contraindications?

Significant co-morbidities, psychosocial considerations, immunological issues, surgical considerations, age

o

  • The ethical principle of “justice” is important, as there are usually too few donors for those who might benefit from the therapy
Post-transplant care
  • Patients are often frail and deconditioned at the time of transplant and require intensive rehabilitation pre-/post-operatively
  • Medical therapy includes immunosuppressive agents – tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone
  • Prophylaxis against opportunistic infections – pneumocystis, CMV
  • Routine endomyocardial biopsies are performed to assess for rejection
Cardiac transplant outcomes
  • Graft half-life: at 12 years, 50% of the hearts are no longer functioning

blocks.alt: Figure from the Cardiac Transplant notes

blocks.html:
• Early deaths: infection, rejection, vasoplegia, cerebrovascular events
  • Later deaths: cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, infection/rejection
  • The number of heart transplantations increased in the mid-1980s – better immunosuppression drugs (cyclosporine)

blocks.alt: Figure from the Cardiac Transplant notes

blocks.html:
Ventricular Assist Devices (VAD)
  • Surgically implanted, electrically driven pump that moves blood from the ventricle(s) into the arterial circulation
  • Durations: temporary and durable
  • Designs: axial and centrifugal

Axial Flow Devices

Centrifugal Flow Devices

Blood travels in the same direction as the rotor’s orientation

Blood enters the pump perpendicular to the orientation of the rotor

Blood can contact static devices – stators

Rotor does not need to contact any static surface – magnetic levitation

  • More sensitive to physiologic changes in afterload due to the 90° entry

Less sensitive to physiological factors like afterload

May provide better ventricular offloading

Physiological changes affect the ability of the device to offload

  • Brands: Heart Mate II and III Devices, HeartWare HVAD

blocks.alt: Figure from the Cardiac Transplant notes
Figure from the Cardiac Transplant notes

blocks.html:
1.Well-positioned and unimpeded pump – inflow cannula, rotor (propeller), outflow cannula

2.Intact driveline – delivers power and operating information to the pump

3.Functioning controller – tells the pump what to do and monitors its operation

4.Power supply – battery or main wall socket

  • Batteries and controller are on the outside of the patient; driveline tunnels into the patient towards the pump
Indications for VADs
  • Bridge to another therapy (temporary to durable VAD) or transplant
  • Destination therapy for non-transplant candidates
  • Patients may not be a candidate for transplant, but may be a candidate for a VAD
VAD complications
  • Foreign body implanted into the patient and provides blood flow in a non-physiologic way – pulseless
  • Driveline infection – most patients will develop this; surface or deep
  • GI bleeding
  • Stroke/intracranial hemorrhage
  • Device thrombosis
  • Pump malfunction

Functions of the electrical system
  • Impulse initiation
  • Failure to initiate an impulse à bradycardia

o

  • Abnormal rapid repetitive initiation à tachycardia

o

  • Impulse conduction
  • Failure to conduct to all parts of the heart à bradycardia (conduction block)

o

  • Circular conduction (short circuit) à tachycardia

o

Automaticity:specialized cardiac tissue has the ability to initiate impulses and spontaneously depolarize

  • SA node determines when and how quickly the heart beats
  • Under normal physiologic stimuli, the heartbeat will accelerate and decelerate – neural control (autonomic input)

Hierarchy of Pacemaker Automaticity

Rate

  • Automaticity can be pathologically suppressed causing bradycardia

Sinus node disease – scarring with age, fibrosis, sick sinus syndrome

o

o

  • Tissues can become automatic under pathologic conditions

Atrial tachycardia – atrial focus rapidly and repetitively fires

o

During myocardial ischemia/infarction, ventricular muscle may develop automaticity and cause ventricular tachycardia

Case Example

A 78-year-old woman is monitored for syncope.

blocks.html:
• This rhythm strip illustrates reduced automaticity resulting in a 6-second pause in HR
  • Initially, the HR is rapid, irregular, with no signs of p-waves (atrial fibrillation)
  • When atrial fibrillation stops, there is nothing happening in the atrium for 6 seconds and there is no escape beat from the junction taking over
  • Suppression of automaticity results in bradycardia, dizziness, and passing out (syncope)
  • A pacemaker may be indicated to depolarize in the 6 second long pause

Re-entry: the re-stimulation of cardiac muscle due to circular conduction abnormalities

  • Impulse conducts abnormally (usually circular around an obstacle) and perpetuates itself
  • Common cause of tachycardia; does NOT cause bradycardia
  • AV re-entry tachycardia in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome

Patients have an extra short circuit in the form of an accessory pathway that

o

Conduction from the sinus node can go normally down the AV node, around the

conduction system in the ventricle, and back up the accessory pathway

Forms a circuit that re-stimulates the AV node creating a heartbeat each time

Caused by the shape of the AP, which has a long recovery phase

repolarization to occur

Prevents re-stimulation of tissue and is anti-tachycardic

Clinical management of SVT
Acute Management

Chronic Management

AV node blockade:

  • Vagal maneuvers – carotid sinus massage
  • IV adenosine – short-lasting, 10 seconds

Restore sinus:

  • Cardioversion
  • Procainamide – slow atrium
  • Ibutilide – slow atrium

• SINUS NODE DYSFUNCTION = PROBLEM WITH THE BATTERYà not enough P waves
  • Degenerative process that becomes more prevalent with aging
1) Sinus bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence
  • Inappropriate response to sympathetic drive – adrenaline, exercise
  • Symptoms: fatigue, exertional limitation
2) Sinus pauses, sinus arrest
  • Intermittent pauses of the SA node
  • Symptoms: presyncope, syncope
3) Conversion pauses
  • Sinus pause triggered by conversion of a tachycardia
Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome
  • Tachy = AF with rapid rates
  • Brady = sinus conversion pauses
  • Management challenges
Sick sinus syndrome (SSS) = symptomatic sinus node dysfunction
  • Treatment of sinus node dysfunction is appropriate (pacemaker)
Asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction ≠ SSS
  • No indication for treatment
  • AV BLOCK = PROBLEM WITH THE WIRINGà normal P waves, not enough QRS complexes
  • Site of block: AV node, infra-nodal (His bundle, bundle branches) – lower levels of block have a worse prognosis
1)First degree AV block: PR interval > 200 ms

2) Second degree AV block: at least 1 non-conducted P wave; more P waves than QRS complexes

  • Group beating: QRS complexes appear to be bunched together in groups
  • Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): gradual PR interval prolongation before block
  • Mobitz type II (Mobitz): no PR prolongation preceding block
  • 2:1 AV block: every second P wave is non-conducted; no consecutive PR intervals to judge whether they are prolonging or fixed

Site of block: AV node or infra-nodal

o

Pacemaker likely indicated

o

3) Third degree AV block: complete AV block; no conducted P waves
  • More P waves than QRS complexes
  • AV dissociation – QRS complexes are regular, PR interval is variable
  • Regular escape rhythm – can be junctional (narrow QRS) or ventricular (wide QRS)
  • Site of block: AV node (> 40 bpm) or infra-nodal (< 40 bpm)
  • Atrial fibrillation with complete AV block: regular QRS with fibrillatory waves at the baseline (normally irregularly irregular)

Torsades de Pointes/polymorphic ventricular tachycardia = long QT interval

  • Usually triggered by a premature ventricular contraction at the same time as the T wave – “R on T phenomenon”

blocks.html:
Bundle branch blocks (BBB)
  • Warning signs of degenerative conduction disease, which may evolve into complete heart block
  • Same number of P waves and QRS complexes because the other bundle branch is still working
  • Wide QRS > 120 ms – left and right bundle branches are depolarizing consecutively instead of together
  • Left bundle branch block = wide QRS, negative in V1
  • Right bundle branch block = wide QRS, positive in V1
  • Left anterior fascicular block = left axis deviation
  • Left posterior fascicular block = right axis deviation
Bradycardia management
  • Treat for mortality (risk of sudden death): 2nd degree AV block type II, 3rd degree AV block
  • Treat for morbidity (symptomatic): sinus node dysfunction, 2nd degree AV block type I
  • No need for treatment (asymptomatic): sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, Mobitz type I Wenckebach, 1st degree AV block, BBB
Acute Treatment

Chronic Treatment

IV atropine (anti-cholinergic): ↑ HR, improve conduction
IV isoproterenol (sympathomimetic): ↑ HR, improve conduction
Temporary transcutaneous pacing: pads stimulate heart through chest wall
Temporary transvenous pacing wire: through the jugular vein into the RV

Presyncope: a sensation of impending loss of consciousness without progression to loss of consciousness

  • Dizzy, lightheaded; needs to be differentiated from vertigo
  • May be caused by a less severe manifestation of a reduction in cerebral blood flow
Prodrome: the symptoms that precede syncope

Syncope: a transient loss of consciousness (LOC) with spontaneous recovery that does not require intervention

  • Blackout, faint, spell, collapse; not the same as coma, cardiac arrest, drowsiness, generalized seizure
  • Usually due to a reduction in cerebral blood flow (hypotension)

blocks.html:
Clinical presentation of vasovagal syncope
Step

Considerations

Hx

Common situations:

  • Post-prandial, warm day, prolonged standing
  • Post-exertion, post-cough, post-micturition
  • Triggered by pain, anxiety, stress, illness

Prodrome: fatigue, weakness, nausea, sweating, pallor, visual disturbance, abdominal discomfort – seconds-hours before the episode

Post-episode: fatigue, malaise – cardiac syncope with heart block could feel back to their normal self after the episode

Ix

ECG

Absence of QRS complexes – heart is affected by the vasovagal reflex, does not cause it

Parasympathetic affects both the sinus node and AV node at the same time

  • Sinus node = P waves slow down
  • AV node = Wenckebach or AV block

Simultaneous sinus slowing and heart block is diagnostic of a vasovagal reflex

Tilt table test

Vasovagal reflexts affects the systemic vascular resistance – BP decreases

Pure vasodepressor – HR remains stable

Cardioinhibitory/mixed – HR also drops

Management

Lifestyle measures:

  • Reassurance – VVS is generally benign (simply a bodily reflex)
  • Treatment of VVS is salt (electrolytes) and water (hydration)
  • Trigger avoidance

Counter-pressure maneuvers:

  • Feeling a prodrome – do NOT stand to “walk it off”
  • Sit/lie down
  • Squeeze/cross the legs to increase perfusion to the brain

Drug therapy:

  • Beta blockers – blocks SNS overdrive that leads to the reflex PNS surge
  • Fludrocortisone – retain salt in the kidney, increase BP
  • Midodrine – increases vascular resistance and increases BP

Pacemaker:

  • Generally not warranted; given in rare instances – refractory patients; occupations where a vasovagal event puts the patient at high risk
  • Often still faint because pacemakers only addresses the cardioinhibitory component (not the vasodepressor component)
  • Surgical placebo is very effective at treating VVS
Clinical presentation of cardiac syncope
Step

Considerations

Hx
Initial

Routine bloodwork

screening

ECG

Echocardiogram; cardiac MRI or CT if high suspicion – structural heart disease increases risk of malignant arrhythmia

Ambulatory

Patients often seen AFTER the event – only useful if the patient has another episode of syncope during the monitoring period

monitoring

Symptom-rhythm correlation

  • Diagnose the arrhythmia causes of syncope – bradycardia, tachycardia

Monitors – patient should be recording a proper symptoms diary to compare to the rhythm

  • Holter (24-48 hours)
  • External loop recorder
  • Implantable loop recorder – 2-3 year battery life
Provocation

Tilt test

Stress test

Drug infusions

Electrophysiology testing (invasive)

  • Catheters inserted into the heart through the veins; stimulate patient and measure electrical activity
  • Look for signs of conduction disease or the ability to provoke tachycardia rhythms
Management

Treat the underlying cardiac condition:

  • Structural: surgical correction of the obstruction
  • Bradycardia: pacemaker
  • Tachycardia: medications, cardiac ablation, implantable defibrillator

Red flags that warrant additional investigations
Exertional syncope

If someone faints while they exercise, this is NOT vasovagal syncope

Suggest cardiac causes – obstruction and arrythmia can be provoked by exertion/increased demand

Aortic stenosis

3 year survival after the onset of symptoms

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Diagnosed with an echocardiogram

Cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy people

Inherited arrhythmias

FHx of sudden death can point to arrhythmia

  • Long QT syndrome or syncopal events can lead to Torsades de Pointes – triggered by alarm clocks and swimming
  • Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (bidirectional) – triggered by exercise
Sudden syncope

“What was the last thing you remember before fainting?”

  • No memory of any problem is sudden syncope
  • Injury associated with syncopal event is often a sign that the syncope was sudden, and they could not protect themselves
  • Feeling unwell before fainting is not sudden syncope
Structural heart disease

Known CAD, prior MI, poor LVEF

Abnormal ECG

Risk of bradycardia: conduction system disease – LBBB, RBBB, 1st degree AV block

Risk of tachycardia: structural heart disease – Q waves, long QT, WPW (delta waves), Brugada syndrome

1.

Where does the impulse for each heartbeat usually occur? Sinus (SA) node

2.

What structure in the atrial septum slows conduction before it enters the His Purkinje fibres to conduct through the ventricles? Atrioventricular (AV) node

3.

What condition consists of lack of normal automaticity and impulse formation, leading to pauses or junctional escape rhythms? Sinus bradycardia

4.

When ventricular tissue is partly depolarized due to infarction, it can cause increased automaticity and a rhythm called? Ventricular tachycardia

5.

Name 3 tachycardias caused by re-entry: AV re-entrant tachycardia (AV node and accessory pathway); AV node re-entrant tachycardia; scar-related

ventricular tachycardia

6.

What type of beat is required to initiate a re-entrant circuit? An early beat, or premature atrial contraction (PAC), that blocks in one limb of the circuit

and conducts down the other limb

7.

What needs to differ between the two limbs of a re-entrant circuit in order to perpetuate re-entry? Conduction velocity and refractory periods

8.

In ventricular tachycardia in a patient with a remote MI, what are the two limbs of the circuit? Through the scar (slow conduction, short refractoriness)

and around the scar (rapid conduction, longer refractoriness)

blocks.html:
ECG manifestations of atrial fibrillation
  • Multiple re-entrant circuits meander through the atria – multiple waves in atrium
  • Fibrillatory waves – disorganized, continuous; can be very small
  • Irregular RR intervals; irregularly irregular ventricular rate
Etiology of atrial fibrillation
  • Age-dependent with increasing risk after 50; 10% of those 80+ years have atrial fibrillation
  • Cardiac causes: hypertension, ischemic heart disease, valvular heart disease (MS, MR, AS), sick sinus syndrome, cardiomyopathy

(dilated, hypertrophic)

  • Non-cardiac causes: alcohol, metabolic (thyroid disease), pulmonary (COPD, pneumonia sleep apnea)
  • Reversal of underlying disease can make atrial fibrillation easier to treat
Classification of patient presentation
Paroxysmal AF

Highly symptomatic self-terminating episodes; minutes to hours in duration

Patients are well when they return to sinus rhythm

Persistent AF

Does not stop spontaneously – antiarrhythmic agents or DC cardioversion is required

Chronic AF

Patients are in atrial fibrillation all the time – agents are used to slow the ventricular rate and control symptoms

(permanent)

No attempt is made to return these patients to sinus rhythm

Pathophysiology of atrial fibrillation and therapy
1) Thromboembolic events
  • Rapid and chaotic atrial activation leads to disorganized mechanical function and stasis of blood
  • Causes of AF also cause left atrial enlargement and contribute to the stasis of blood
  • Once formed, clots can embolize, causing stroke and other thromboembolic events
  • CHADS2 score: CHF (1), hypertension (1), age > 65 years (1), diabetes (1), prior stroke or TIA (2)
  • Mitral stenosis is also a very high risk factor for stroke
  • Stroke prophylaxis (any 1 risk factor): anti-coagulation (warfarin) or anti-platelet therapy (ASA)

blocks.alt: Figure from the Atrial Fibrillation notes

blocks.html:
2) Rapid irregular ventricular rate
  • The AV node allows rapid activation of the ventricles; rate = 130-170 bpm
  • Symptoms: palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort
  • Tx: rate control with AV nodal blocking drugs – beta blockers, CCB, digoxin
  • AF can result in normal rate or bradycardia; therapy to slow the ventricular rate may or may not be necessary depending on the

function of the AV node

3) Loss of atrial-ventricular synchrony
  • Loss of mechanical function of the atria prevents the atrial contribution to ventricular filling – atrial kick
  • In some heart diseases, the loss of atrial kick can reduce LV filling, cardiac output, and lead to symptoms of breathlessness,

exertional dyspnea, and fatigue

  • Tx: rhythm control– antiarrhythmic drugs, DC cardioversion

Class I agents (Na+ channel blockade): flecainide, propafenone

o

Class III agents (K+ channel blockade): sotalol, amiodarone, dronedarone

o

DC cardioversion: electrical synchronized shock to return AF to sinus
  • Patient anaesthetized (propofol), paddles placed anterior and

posterior, shock delivered (50-200 J), patient awakes in sinus rhythm

  • AF < 48 hours with no anti-coagulation is okay
  • AF > 48 hours (or unknown) – rate control until 3 weeks of anti-

coagulation prior to cardioversion (risk of thrombus formation)

blocks.html:
Case Example
  • A 42-year-old man is in the ER with rapid palpitations and dyspnea for 12 hours
  • History of hypertension for years on Enalapril
  • ECG showed rapid atrial fibrillation (140-160 bpm)
  • BP = 110/85

blocks.alt: Figure from the Antiarrhythmic Pharmacology notes

blocks.html:
• Changing the slope of phase 0 à widening of the QRS complex
  • Prolonging the plateau phase à prolong QT interval
Basic principles of therapy
1) Identify and treat the precipitating factors
  • Electrolyte abnormalities – low K+, Mg2+, PO43–
  • Myocardial ischemia
  • Hypoxemia
  • Catecholamines – endogenous (anxiety, pain, fever), exogenous (epinephrine, dopamine)
  • Other modifiable risk factors – weight reduction, alcohol consumption, smoking cessation
  • Medications – drugs may prolong QT; antiarrhythmics may have a proarrhythmic effect
2) Decide on your goal
  • Not all arrhythmias need treatment – sinus tachycardia (treat underlying cause)
  • Atrial fibrillation – rate control vs. restore sinus rhythm; thrombosis prophylaxis if indicated
3) Minimize risk
  • Drug-drug interactions
  • Renal dysfunction – many medications are renally excreted; be aware of renal function and pharmacology of the medication to

avoid increased side effects or toxicity

  • Non-pharmacologic therapy may be the most appropriate – pacemaker, internal cardiac defibrillator

Proarrhythmia: the ability of drugs (including antiarrhythmics) to cause arrhythmias

  • Digoxin – toxicity may lead to virtually any arrhythmia, including triggered activity
  • Drugs that prolong QT – Torsades de Pointes
  • Drug-induced bradyarrhythmia – beta blockers, CCB

Based on the ECG, what is the diagnosis?

a)

  • Atrial fibrillationà narrow complex and irregularly irregular

b)

  • Supraventricular tachycardia à narrow complex and regular

c)

  • Atrial flutter à flutter or “F waves” in the inferior leads

d)

  • Ventricular tachycardia à wide complex and regular

The patient is identified to be in atrial fibrillation with heart rate of 110 bpm when examined in the office. Her physical examination is otherwise unremarkable

with no murmurs or elevated JVP.

Her blood pressure is 130/80. At present she feels well and is not complaining of any symptoms but is concerned by the new diagnosis

An echocardiogram is ordered and ultimately shows no evidence of structural disease.

What would be the next appropriate steps in treating this patient?

a)

Anticoagulate

b)

Beta-blocker for rate control

c)

Anti-arrhythmic Medication

d)

Elective electrical cardioversion

e)

A and B

For THIS PATIENT is A + B: anticoagulation and beta blocker for rate control. It is important to note however, that all answers can be acceptable treatment

solutions in certain situations. This question highlights 2 key treatment principles for atrial fibrillation – (1) need for anticoagulation and (2) rate vs rhythm

control.

For patients with AF – stroke risk is determined by using a risk model called the CHADS2 score. In this patient’s case her score would be 2 based on age and

hypertension for an annual stroke risk of 4%.

Given that the patient is otherwise relatively stable, and her AF is a new finding, there would be no need for emergency cardioversion or use of an anti-

arrhythmic medication urgently. Rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker is a good first step, as it will control the ventricular rate during

exercise. Also given that the duration of AF is unknown and could be greater than 48 hours, the risk of thrombus is high, hence the need for anticoagulation. If

the duration of atrial fibrillation is, or may be, greater than 48 hours and the patient is not on appropriate anticoagulation, cardioversion should only be

performed in the setting of hemodynamic instability, or if an intra-cardiac thrombus is excluded by imaging (i.e. transesophageal echocardiogram).
